items.stem: Which material is used for cutlery because it does not rust?
items.answer: stainless steel
items.markingKey: Chromium and nickel stop the iron rusting.

items.stem: What is galvanising?
options: Coating iron with a layer of zinc
items.answer: Coating iron with a layer of zinc
items.markingKey: Zinc gives barrier and sacrificial protection.

items.stem: Hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, is heated in a test-tube. Describe what you would observe and write the equation for the change.
items.answer: Colourless crystals turn to a white powder; droplets of colourless liquid (water) condense near the top of the tube. Na₂CO₃·10H₂O(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + 10H₂O(g)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: colour/appearance change; 1 mark: condensation of water; 1 mark: equation [2]

items.stem: Aqueous chlorine is added to aqueous potassium bromide. What is observed?
options: the solution turns brown as iodine is formed
no change; the solution stays the colour of the halogen solution
the colourless solution turns orange as bromine is formed
items.answer: the colourless solution turns orange as bromine is formed

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how increased greenhouse gas emissions lead to climate change. (b) Explain why catalytic converters work only once the engine is warm.
items.answer: (a) More CO₂/CH₄ absorbs and re-emits more thermal energy towards Earth, raising average temperatures, which changes weather patterns, melts ice and raises sea levels. (b) The catalyst needs a high temperature to work effectively.

items.stem: In a titration, the initial burette reading is 1.65 cm³ and the final reading is 22.40 cm³. Calculate the titre and state the precision to which burette readings are recorded.
items.answer: 20.75 cm³; to the nearest 0.05 cm³

items.stem: Why is universal indicator not used in titrations?
options: It changes colour gradually over a range of pH, so the end-point is not sharp
items.answer: It changes colour gradually over a range of pH, so the end-point is not sharp
items.markingKey: A single sharp colour change is needed.

items.stem: State the order of reactivity of copper, iron and magnesium, most reactive first.
items.answer: magnesium > iron > copper

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation. (b) Explain why PET can be recycled into new PET by converting it back to monomers.
items.answer: (a) Addition: alkene monomers join, polymer is the only product. Condensation: monomers with two functional groups join, eliminating water (or HCl). (b) The ester links can be broken (hydrolysed/depolymerised) to regenerate the monomers, which are then repolymerised.

items.stem: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethane?
items.answer: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O

items.stem: Deduce whether ethyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₃, and butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, are structural isomers. Explain your answer.
items.answer: No: their molecular formulae differ (C₃H₆O₂ and C₄H₁₀O).
items.markingKey: 1 mark molecular formulae compared; 1 mark conclusion [1]

items.stem: Calculate the volume of hydrogen, in cm³ at r.t.p., produced when 0.360 g of magnesium reacts with excess dilute sulfuric acid. Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂
items.answer: 360 cm³

items.stem: Why is aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite?
options: To provide oxygen for the anode
To lower the operating temperature and improve conductivity
items.answer: To lower the operating temperature and improve conductivity
items.markingKey: Al₂O₃ melts above 2000 °C; the solution in cryolite works at about 950 °C, saving energy.

items.stem: After precipitation, how is the insoluble salt separated from the mixture?
items.answer: filtration
items.markingKey: The precipitate stays as residue on the filter paper.

items.stem: Argon is used for filling filament lamps and as a shield gas in welding. Explain which property makes it suitable.
items.answer: It is unreactive, so the hot metal does not react with oxygen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark property; 1 mark link to use [1]

items.stem: Approximately what volume of oxygen is present in 2400 dm³ of clean, dry air?
items.answer: 504 dm³

items.stem: During a separation, Omar heated the solution to dryness to make crystals. Explain what is wrong and how to correct it.
items.answer: This gives powder/decomposition and removes water of crystallisation; heat to saturation and cool.

items.stem: A gas is produced from magnesium and dilute sulfuric acid. Name the gas and describe a test to confirm its identity, giving the result.
items.answer: hydrogen; a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
items.markingKey: 1 mark gas; 1 mark test; 1 mark result [2]

items.stem: State the general rule used to predict whether a displacement reaction will happen.
items.answer: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compounds (solution or oxide).

items.stem: A council in Mumbai is choosing between recycling and incineration for its plastic waste. Give one disadvantage of each.
items.answer: Recycling: requires the plastics to be collected and sorted, and some types cannot be recycled. Incineration: produces carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) and toxic gases such as hydrogen chloride from PVC.

items.stem: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of butan-1-ol.
items.answer: C₄H₉OH + 6O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O

items.stem: Deduce whether methane, CH₄, and propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, belong to the same homologous series. Explain your answer.
items.answer: No: methane is an alkane (C–C single bonds only) but propanoic acid is a carboxylic acid (–COOH (carboxyl)).
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark functional group/general formula reasoning [2]

items.stem: A manufacturer in Accra makes silver-coloured coins from cupronickel, an alloy of copper and nickel. (a) State what is meant by an alloy. (b) Suggest why cupronickel is suitable for silver-coloured coins.
items.answer: (a) A mixture of a metal with other elements. (b) Hard, hard-wearing and resistant to corrosion.

items.stem: A blast furnace is charged with 40 t of hematite and 25.2 t of iron is tapped off. Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the percentage by mass of iron(III) oxide in the ore.
Diego predicts that potassium carbonate, K₂CO₃, is insoluble in water. Use the solubility rules to explain whether Diego is correct.
items.answer: Diego is incorrect: potassium carbonate is soluble because all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct conclusion (soluble); 1 mark: rule quoted (all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble) [2]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of iron in Fe₂O₃ and hence name the compound using a Roman numeral.
items.answer: +3; iron(III) compound
items.markingKey: Oxidation numbers in a compound sum to zero; O = −2, Cl = −1, K = +1, SO₄ = −2, NO₃ = −1, OH = −1 [1]; iron = +3 [1]

items.stem: Water samples from a coastal bay in Cairo contain plastics. Explain why this is a problem.
items.answer: Harm aquatic life that eats them or becomes trapped.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies harm; 1 mark explains how [2]

items.stem: Leila uses paper chromatography to test a black ink. Known dyes blue, yellow, red are spotted next to the ink. The solvent front moves 10 cm. The ink gives two spots, at 4.5 cm and 2.5 cm; the known dyes travel blue 4.5 cm, yellow 7.0 cm, red 2.5 cm. (a) Calculate the Rf values of the two spots in the ink. (b) Explain why the solvent level must be below the baseline.
items.answer: (a) 0.45 and 0.25 (b) Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.

items.stem: Acidified aqueous silver nitrate is added to a solution and a cream precipitate forms. Identify the ion and write the ionic equation with state symbols.
items.answer: bromide (Br⁻); Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark ion; 1 mark equation; 1 mark state symbols [3]

items.stem: Pb + 2Ag⁺ → Pb²⁺ + 2Ag. Use ideas about electron transfer to explain which species is oxidised and which is reduced, and why this shows lead is more reactive than silver.
items.answer: Lead atoms lose electrons (oxidised) to form ions; silver ions gain electrons (reduced) to form atoms. Lead has the greater tendency to form positive ions, so it is more reactive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark oxidised species; 1 mark reduced species; 1 mark link to tendency to form positive ions [3]

items.stem: Name the polymer formed from propene and give one use.
items.answer: poly(propene); ropes, crates and food containers

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why ethanoic acid reacts more slowly with magnesium than hydrochloric acid of the same concentration. (b) Explain why esterification is described as a condensation reaction.
items.answer: (a) Ethanoic acid is a weak acid — only partially dissociated — so the concentration of H⁺ ions is lower. (b) Two molecules join together and a small molecule (water) is eliminated.

items.stem: Four organic compounds are: A CH₃OH; B CH₃COOH; C CH₄; D CH₃CH₂OH. (a) Which compound(s) would react with sodium carbonate to give carbon dioxide? (b) Name the ester that could be made from methanol and ethanoic acid, and give its structural formula.
items.answer: (a) B (b) methyl ethanoate; CH₃COOCH₃

items.stem: Felix reads that lead is extracted from lead(II) oxide by heating it with carbon. (a) Explain why lead can be extracted using carbon. (b) 500 kg of ore contains 60% PbO. Calculate the maximum mass of lead produced. (c) Suggest one environmental problem caused by extracting metals from ores.
items.answer: (a) Carbon is more reactive than lead, so it can remove oxygen from PbO. (b) 278 kg (c) Mining scars the landscape/habitat loss; CO₂ from burning coke contributes to climate change; waste rock.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) mass PbO = 300 kg [1]; n = 1.35 kmol [1]; mass lead = 278 kg [1]; total [3] (c) [1]

items.stem: Elena titrates 20.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide with 0.0800 mol/dm³ nitric acid using thymolphthalein indicator. Burette readings / cm³ — rough: initial 0.50, final 27.80; titration 1: initial 3.10, final 29.50; titration 2: initial 0.50, final 26.85; titration 3: initial 3.10, final 29.45. (a) Calculate each titre and identify the concordant results. (b) State the colour change at the end-point. (c) Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide. NaOH + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O
items.answer: (a) 27.30; 26.40; 26.35; 26.35 cm³; concordant: 26.40, 26.35, 26.35 (b) blue to colourless (c) 0.105 mol/dm³
items.markingKey: (a) titre = final − initial for each [1]; concordant = within 0.10 cm³, rough excluded [1]; total [2] (b) [1] (c) n(acid) = 26.37/1000 × 0.0800 = 0.00211 mol [1]; n(alkali) = 0.00211 mol [1]; c = 0.00211 ÷ 0.0200 = 0.105 mol/dm³ [1]; total [3]

items.stem: Nadia watches a teacher add a small piece of potassium to a trough of water containing a few drops of universal indicator. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction with water. (b) Explain, in terms of atomic structure, why potassium is more reactive than lithium. (c) Suggest one safety precaution needed for this demonstration. (d) State the formula of the ion formed by potassium and explain its charge.
items.answer: (a) 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂ (b) Potassium has more electron shells; its outer electron is further from the nucleus and less strongly attracted, so it is lost more easily. (c) Use a very small piece / safety screen / goggles / tongs, not fingers. (d) K⁺: it loses its single outer electron.

items.stem: A fertiliser factory in Muscat makes ammonium nitrate by reacting ammonia with nitric acid. (a) Write the balanced equation for the formation of the fertiliser. (b) Explain why this fertiliser should not be mixed with calcium hydroxide. (c) State which other element(s) a farmer might need to add, and suggest a compound to supply it.
items.answer: (a) NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃ (b) Calcium hydroxide is an alkali; it reacts with ammonium ions to release ammonia gas, losing nitrogen. (c) Potassium (e.g. potassium nitrate/sulfate) and phosphorus (e.g. ammonium phosphate).

items.stem: Lucas is given a solution of ethanol, water and a dissolved coloured dye and asked to obtain pure samples of the components. (a) Describe a method to separate the components. (b) Define the terms solute and solvent. (c) Describe how you could show that the water collected is pure.
items.answer: (a) fractional distillation to collect ethanol at 78 °C; then water at 100 °C; dye left in flask; check purity by chromatography. (b) Solute: substance that dissolves; solvent: liquid in which it dissolves. (c) Measure its boiling point: 100 °C exactly (or freezing point 0 °C).

items.stem: Amara is given an unlabelled solution of a salt in a sixth-form practical class and tests it with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia. (a) The solution gave a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution. Identify the cation, explaining your reasoning. (b) Predict what would be seen with aqueous ammonia. (c) Describe how to carry out a flame test.
items.answer: (a) Al³⁺ (aluminium) — confirm with aqueous ammonia (b) white precipitate, insoluble in excess (c) Dip a clean nichrome wire (cleaned with conc. HCl) into the solid, hold in a blue Bunsen flame, observe colour.

items.stem: A teacher in Muscat demonstrates the preparation of iron(II) nitrate from iron and 100 cm³ of nitric acid of concentration 2.00 mol/dm³. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction. (b) Describe how you would know that the solid is in excess. (c) Calculate the number of moles of nitric acid used. (d) Calculate the maximum mass of Fe(NO₃)₂ (Mr = 180) that can form. (e) The percentage yield was 85%. Calculate the mass of crystals obtained and suggest one reason why the yield is less than 100%.
items.answer: (a) Fe + 2HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + H₂ (b) Solid remains undissolved and effervescence stops. (c) 0.200 mol (d) 18.0 g (e) 15.3 g; e.g. some salt remains dissolved in the solution after crystallisation / losses on transfer.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balanced [2] (b) [1] (c) n = 100/1000 × 2.00 [1] (d) n(salt) = 0.100 mol; mass = 0.100 × 180 = 18.0 g [2] (e) mass = 85/100 × 18.0 [1]; reason [1]; total [2]

items.stem: The table gives the electronic configurations of five elements (letters are not symbols): Q 2,2; R 2,8,2; T 2,8,8,1; X 2,7; Z 2,8,7. (a) Predict the charge on the ion formed by T, if any. (b) Which two elements would have similar chemical properties? Explain. (c) Name the element X.
items.answer: (a) +1 (b) X and Z: same number of outer electrons (same group). (c) fluorine

items.stem: Hana draws a labelled diagram of a fractionating column showing where three fractions, bitumen, gasoline / petrol, fuel oil, are collected. (a) Describe how fractional distillation separates petroleum. (b) Give a use of gasoline / petrol. (c) Give one reason why burning fossil fuels causes environmental concern.
items.answer: (a) Petroleum is heated to vaporise it; the column is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top; fractions condense at different heights according to boiling point. (b) fuel for cars (c) CO₂ is a greenhouse gas (climate change); SO₂ causes acid rain; CO/particulates from incomplete combustion.

items.stem: An oil refinery in Lisbon cracks C₁₂H₂₆ to make petrol and ethene. (a) State the conditions needed for cracking. (b) Name the product when ethene reacts with bromine and state the type of reaction. (c) Suggest why hydrogen is also a useful product of some cracking reactions.
items.answer: (a) High temperature (about 500 °C) and a catalyst (e.g. aluminium oxide/silica). (b) 1,2-dibromoethane; addition (c) It can be used as a fuel or to make ammonia/margarine.

items.stem: A bottle in a chemistry club is labelled "but-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃". (a) Name the homologous series and the functional group. (b) Calculate the relative molecular mass. (c) Describe what the displayed formula would show. (d) Name the next member of the same homologous series and give its formula.
items.answer: (a) alkene; C=C double bond (b) 56 (c) Every atom and every covalent bond; each carbon with four bonds. (d) pent-1-ene, C₅H₁₀

items.stem: Engineers are reviewing the materials used for overhead power cables in a new factory. (a) State the property of aluminium that makes it suitable for overhead power cables. (b) Explain how this property relates to the structure of aluminium. (c) Data: aluminium density 2.7 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion; zinc density 7.14 g/cm³, corrosion — corrodes slowly; brass density 8.5 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion. Identify the least dense metal and suggest one use that benefits from its low density. (d) Suggest one disadvantage of using pure iron for an outdoor structure and how steel overcomes it.
items.answer: (a) low density and good electrical conductivity (b) Metallic structure: delocalised electrons give conductivity; layers of ions give malleability/ductility; oxide layer or alloying gives corrosion resistance. (c) aluminium; e.g. aircraft bodies or vehicle parts, to reduce mass (it also resists corrosion). (d) Iron rusts and is soft; stainless steel resists rusting and is harder (or mild steel is stronger and can be painted).

items.stem: Mateo sets up four test-tubes to investigate rusting and leaves them for one week. tube 1: an iron nail wrapped in a strip of magnesium, in tap water; tube 2: an iron nail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride; tube 3: an iron nail in boiled water covered with a layer of oil; tube 4: an iron nail in tap water, open to the air. (a) Predict in which tubes the nail rusts. (b) Describe how boiling the water and adding oil changes the conditions.
items.answer: (a) 4 (b) Boiling removes dissolved oxygen; the oil layer stops oxygen from the air redissolving.

items.stem: Aisha investigates hydrated iron(II) sulfate, FeSO₄·xH₂O. A 5.56 g sample is heated in a crucible; its mass is recorded after each heating: 4.17 g, 3.42 g, 3.04 g, 3.04 g. (a) Explain why the sample was heated several times. (b) Suggest how the calculated value of x would be affected if the sample was not heated to constant mass.
items.answer: (a) To make sure all the water of crystallisation was removed — heating to constant mass. (b) x would be too small, because less water would appear to have been lost.

items.stem: Aqueous chlorine is added to aqueous sodium iodide. Predict whether a reaction occurs. If it does, describe the colour change and write the balanced symbol equation and the ionic equation.
items.answer: Yes — the colourless solution turns brown as iodine is formed. Cl₂ + 2NaI → 2NaCl + I₂; ionic: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂
items.markingKey: 1 mark: reaction because chlorine is more reactive; 1 mark: colour; 1 mark: equation; 1 mark ionic equation [4]

items.stem: A city council plans to cut air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions over the next ten years. (a) Name two pollutants removed by a catalytic converter. (b) Write the balanced equation for photosynthesis and explain how it affects the atmosphere.
items.answer: (a) Carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen (also unburned hydrocarbons). (b) 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; it removes CO₂ and adds O₂.

items.stem: Ana investigates the reaction of marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of carbon dioxide produced every 20 s. Results (time / s, volume / cm³): 0, 0; 20, 41; 40, 64; 60, 78; 80, 86; 100, 90. (a) Name the apparatus used to measure time. (b) State and explain how the rate changes during the experiment. (c) Suggest how the volume of acid should be measured, and why. (d) Identify one variable that must be controlled.
items.answer: (a) Stop-watch. (b) Rate decreases: the concentration of acid (and amount of solid) falls, so collisions are less frequent. (c) Measuring cylinder is adequate (the acid is in excess) — or a pipette/burette for greater accuracy. (d) Temperature, concentration/volume of acid, or mass/surface area of the solid.

items.stem: Ines determines the concentration of sodium hydroxide by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.120 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid, using methyl orange. Burette readings (initial → final, cm³): rough: 0.00 → 20.50; run 1: 2.35 → 22.15; run 2: 3.10 → 22.95; run 3: 1.05 → 20.85. (a) State the colour change at the end-point. (b) Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O (c) Explain why universal indicator is not suitable. (d) Explain why the rough titre is not included in the mean.
items.answer: (a) yellow to red (b) 0.190 mol/dm³ (c) It changes colour gradually; no sharp end-point. (d) It overshoots/ is only approximate.

items.stem: Felix investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; Q: cold water — reacts vigorously, fizzing and moving around on the surface; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; R: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; S: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) S is iron. Write the equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid. (c) Predict what would happen if R were added to a solution of copper(II) sulfate. Explain. (d) Name the gas produced when metals react with dilute acids and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) R > Q > S > P (b) Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂ (c) It reacts with the water first: fizzing (hydrogen) and an alkaline hydroxide forms, giving a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide; copper metal is not displaced. (d) Hydrogen — lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

items.stem: Which ion is present if a solid fizzes with dilute acid and the gas turns limewater milky?
items.answer: carbonate

items.stem: What forms at the cathode during the electrolysis of aluminium oxide?
items.answer: aluminium
items.markingKey: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al at the negative electrode.

items.stem: An unknown element E has these properties — appearance: dull; effect of hammering: brittle (when solid); electrical conductivity: poor (except graphite). Deduce whether E is a metal or a non-metal, explaining your reasoning using each property.
items.answer: Non-metal: dull appearance is typical of a non-metal; brittle (when solid) effect of hammering is typical of a non-metal; poor (except graphite) electrical conductivity is typical of a non-metal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark per property correctly linked, max [3]

items.stem: What is the relative formula mass of CaCl₂·6H₂O?
Describe the displayed formula of propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, stating the number and type of each bond that would be drawn.
items.answer: All atoms shown with every bond: one C=C double bond, 1 C–C single bond(s) and 6 C–H bonds; each C has four bonds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark all bonds shown (each C four bonds); 1 mark correct bond counts [2]

items.stem: A water company in Colombo takes water from a river that flows past farmland and a town. Name two pollutants that might be found in the river and their sources.
items.answer: Nitrates/phosphates from fertilisers; sewage from the town; metal compounds from industry; plastics from litter.

items.stem: Which halogen is a grey-black solid at room temperature?
items.answer: iodine
items.markingKey: Iodine is a grey-black solid that gives a purple vapour on warming.

items.stem: What is the purpose of the fractionating column?
options: To separate liquids with close boiling points by repeated condensation and evaporation
items.answer: To separate liquids with close boiling points by repeated condensation and evaporation
items.markingKey: The column has a temperature gradient: the lower-b.p. liquid reaches the top first.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the displacement of copper by magnesium is a redox reaction. (b) Explain why the sulfate ions are described as spectator ions in Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
items.answer: (a) Magnesium atoms lose electrons (oxidised) to form Mg²⁺; copper(II) ions gain electrons (reduced) to form copper atoms. (b) They are present in solution before and after the reaction and are not changed.

items.stem: Which equation shows the complete combustion of ethanol?
items.answer: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

items.stem: Compare PET and nylon in terms of the type of monomers, the linkage formed and the small molecule eliminated.
items.answer: PET: a dicarboxylic acid and a diol, ester (–COO–), water; nylon: a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine, amide (–CONH–), water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark monomers; 1 mark linkage; 1 mark small molecule [3]

items.stem: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution containing copper(II) ions. Describe what is seen, including when excess is added, and write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate.
items.answer: Light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess; Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark colour of precipitate; 1 mark behaviour in excess; 1 mark ionic equation; 1 mark state symbols [4]

items.stem: What is an ore?
options: A pure metal found in the ground
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extraction worthwhile
A mixture of metal and carbon
items.answer: A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extraction worthwhile
items.markingKey: Ores are naturally occurring rocks from which metals are economically extracted.

items.stem: Which element is added to iron to make steel?
items.answer: carbon
items.markingKey: Steel is iron with carbon (and sometimes other metals).

items.stem: Elena predicts that iron(II) nitrate, Fe(NO₃)₂, is insoluble in water. Use the solubility rules to explain whether Elena is correct.
items.answer: Elena is incorrect: iron(II) nitrate is soluble because all nitrates are soluble.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct conclusion (soluble); 1 mark: rule quoted (all nitrates are soluble) [2]

items.stem: Methylpropane has the structural formula CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃. Give the name and structural formula of one structural isomer of methylpropane.
items.answer: butane: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ (any one)
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct structural formula; 1 mark name [2]

items.stem: A government in Jakarta is considering two policies: reducing livestock farming and planting trees. Explain how each would reduce pollution or climate change.
items.answer: Reducing livestock farming: reduces methane emissions. Planting trees: removes CO₂ by photosynthesis.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each policy explained, 1 mark linking to the specific pollutant/gas [3]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of copper in CuO and hence name the compound using a Roman numeral.
items.answer: +2; copper(II) compound
items.markingKey: Oxidation numbers in a compound sum to zero; O = −2, Cl = −1, K = +1, SO₄ = −2, NO₃ = −1, OH = −1 [1]; copper = +2 [1]

items.stem: What is a locating agent used for?
items.answer: To make colourless spots visible
items.markingKey: Spots of colourless substances (e.g. amino acids) are sprayed with a locating agent and appear coloured.

items.stem: Mg + Fe²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Fe. Use ideas about electron transfer to explain which species is oxidised and which is reduced, and why this shows magnesium is more reactive than iron.
items.answer: Magnesium atoms lose electrons (oxidised) to form ions; iron ions gain electrons (reduced) to form atoms. Magnesium has the greater tendency to form positive ions, so it is more reactive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark oxidised species; 1 mark reduced species; 1 mark link to tendency to form positive ions [3]

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of methane, CH₄.
items.answer: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

items.stem: Lina says that poly(phenylethene), polystyrene is an alkene because it is made from phenylethene (styrene). Explain the error.
items.answer: The polymer is saturated: no C=C bonds remain.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies error; 1 mark correct chemistry [2]

items.stem: Leila carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) sodium sulfite warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid; (2) magnesium and dilute sulfuric acid; (3) ammonium chloride warmed with sodium hydroxide. (a) Suggest which gas should only be tested in a fume cupboard and why. (b) Write an equation for reaction (1).
items.answer: (a) Chlorine, sulfur dioxide or ammonia — they are toxic/irritants. (b) Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + SO₂

items.stem: A painted bicycle frame in Madrid is scratched, exposing the iron underneath. Predict whether the iron at the scratch will rust. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Yes: paint is only a barrier; once broken, water and oxygen reach the iron.

items.stem: Explain why copper is used for electrical wiring.
items.answer: Because of its good electrical conductivity and ductility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark property; 1 mark linked to the use [2]

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction between iron(II) oxide and nitric acid to make iron(II) nitrate.
items.answer: FeO + 2HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + H₂O

items.stem: Tomás names CH₃CH₂CH₃ as "propene". Explain the mistake and give the correct name.
items.answer: Correct name: propane. The functional group is C–C single bonds only, so it is an alkane, not an alkene.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies error (chain length or functional group); 1 mark correct name [2]

items.stem: Priya prepares a sample of ammonium sulfate in the laboratory by titrating aqueous ammonia with sulfuric acid. (a) Calculate the mass of nitrogen in a 50 kg bag. (b) Explain why this fertiliser should not be mixed with calcium hydroxide.
items.answer: (a) 10.6 kg (b) Calcium hydroxide is an alkali; it reacts with ammonium ions to release ammonia gas, losing nitrogen.

items.stem: The melting points of some Group I metals are: lithium 181 °C; sodium 98 °C; potassium 63 °C. Predict the melting point of rubidium and describe how its reaction with water would compare with that of potassium.
items.answer: About 39 °C (accept a value consistent with the trend: lower than 63 °C); it reacts more violently/explosively than potassium.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: prediction consistent with trend (melting point decreases down the group); 1 mark: more reactive (explosive) [2]

items.stem: Suggest a method to obtain ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water and explain why it works.
items.answer: Fractional distillation: the liquids have different boiling points (78 °C and 100 °C).

items.stem: Name the ester formed when ethanoic acid reacts with methanol, and state the conditions needed.
items.answer: methyl ethanoate; warm with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst).

items.stem: Compare the diesel oil / gas oil and lubricating oil fractions in terms of chain length, boiling point and where they are collected in the column.
items.answer: Diesel oil / gas oil (C15–C20) has shorter chains, a lower boiling point and is collected higher up the column than lubricating oil (C30–C50).

items.stem: In a titration, 10.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide required 23.85 cm³ of hydrochloric acid for neutralisation. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.0419 mol/dm³

items.stem: A steelworks in Auckland feeds 800 tonnes of hematite ore containing 75% iron(III) oxide into its blast furnace each day. (a) Write the equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide. (b) Calculate the maximum mass of iron produced from 800 tonnes of the ore. (c) Name two gases that leave the top of the furnace.
items.answer: (a) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (b) 420 tonnes (c) Nitrogen and carbon dioxide (also some carbon monoxide).

items.stem: Mateo prepares zinc carbonate by mixing 40.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ zinc chloride with an excess of aqueous sodium carbonate. (a) Calculate the maximum mass of precipitate (Mr = 125). (b) The dry mass obtained was 0.800 g. Calculate the percentage yield and suggest one reason why it is below 100%. (c) Explain why zinc chloride is used rather than zinc hydroxide as the source of zinc ions.
items.answer: (a) 1.00 g (b) 80.0%; some solid lost on the filter paper or in transfer. (c) Zinc chloride is soluble so it provides free zinc ions; the alternative is insoluble.

items.stem: A student plots the boiling points of the first five alkanes against the number of carbon atoms. Data: methane −162 °C; ethane −89 °C; propane −42 °C; butane −1 °C; pentane 36 °C. (a) State the general formula of the alkanes. (b) Describe the trend shown. (c) Explain the trend. (d) Give two other characteristics of a homologous series. (e) Write the molecular formula of hexane.
items.answer: (a) CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (b) Boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases. (c) Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, needing more energy to separate. (d) Same functional group; similar chemical properties; differ by CH₂; same general formula. (e) C₆H₁₄

items.stem: The table gives the electronic configurations of five elements (letters are not symbols): Q 2,8,3; R 2,4; T 2,8,6; X 2,2; Z 2,8,5. (a) Which elements are in the same period as Q? (b) Which elements are metals? Explain how you decided. (c) Explain why none of these elements would have closely similar chemical properties. (d) Name the element X.
items.answer: (a) T, Z (b) Q, X: they have 1, 2 or 3 outer electrons (left of the table) and lose them to form positive ions. (c) They all have different numbers of outer electrons, so they are in different groups. (d) beryllium
items.markingKey: (a) same number of shells [1] (b) 1 mark letters; 1 mark reason [2] (c) [2] (d) [1]

items.stem: Tomás titrates 25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide with 0.200 mol/dm³ nitric acid using thymolphthalein indicator. Burette readings / cm³ — rough: initial 3.10, final 27.20; titration 1: initial 0.00, final 23.15; titration 2: initial 3.10, final 26.30; titration 3: initial 1.05, final 24.15. (a) Calculate the mean titre using the concordant results. (b) State the colour change at the end-point. (c) Explain why the rough titration is not used in calculating the mean. (d) Describe how you would then obtain pure dry crystals of potassium nitrate.
items.answer: (a) 23.15 cm³ (b) blue to colourless (c) It is only to find the approximate end-point; the acid is added quickly so it usually overshoots. (d) Repeat the titration with the same volumes but no indicator; heat the solution to the point of crystallisation; cool; filter and dry crystals.

items.stem: A report compares the air in a quiet rural village with the air in a busy industrial city. (a) State the composition of clean, dry air. (b) Describe the source of methane. (c) Write an equation for the formation of nitrogen monoxide in a car engine. (d) Explain how carbon dioxide is linked to the source you would expect near a busy road.
items.answer: (a) 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, about 1% noble gases (mainly argon) and 0.04% carbon dioxide. (b) Decomposition of vegetation and waste gases from digestion in animals. (c) N₂ + O₂ → 2NO (d) Complete combustion of carbon-containing fuels; traffic burns large amounts of fuel.

items.stem: A lighting company in Seoul uses argon in its products. (a) Explain why argon is unreactive. (b) State why argon is described as monatomic. (c) Explain why argon is suitable for filling filament lamps and as a shield gas in welding. (d) Predict whether argon has a higher or lower boiling point than neon. (e) Suggest how noble gases are obtained from the air.
items.answer: (a) Its outer shell is full, so it does not need to lose, gain or share electrons. (b) It exists as single atoms, not molecules. (c) It is unreactive, so the hot metal does not react with oxygen. (d) higher (e) By fractional distillation of liquid air.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) [1] (c) [2] (d) boiling point increases down the group [1] (e) [1]

items.stem: Sofia investigates the reaction of zinc granules with dilute sulfuric acid by measuring the volume of hydrogen produced every 20 s. Results (time / s, volume / cm³): 0, 0; 20, 24; 40, 36; 60, 42; 80, 45; 100, 46. (a) Name the apparatus used to measure the volume of gas. (b) Name the apparatus used to measure time. (c) Identify one variable that must be controlled. (d) Suggest why the results become less reliable if the bung is not inserted quickly.
items.answer: (a) Gas syringe. (b) Stop-watch. (c) Temperature, concentration/volume of acid, or mass/surface area of the solid. (d) Some gas escapes before it can be collected, so readings are too low.

items.stem: Mohammed investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles; Q: cold water — fizzes steadily; the water turns cloudy as calcium hydroxide forms; dilute acid — reacts very vigorously; R: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; S: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test. (a) Suggest how R could be tested with steam and what result you would expect. (b) Name the gas produced when metals react with dilute acids and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) Heat the metal strongly in a tube while passing steam over it; no reaction expected. (b) Hydrogen — lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

items.stem: An oil refinery in Colombo cracks C₁₂H₂₆ to make petrol and ethene. (a) Write the balanced equation for cracking C₁₂H₂₆ into C₁₀H₂₂ and ethene. (b) Explain why cracking is needed. (c) Suggest why hydrogen is also a useful product of some cracking reactions.
items.answer: (a) C₁₂H₂₆ → C₁₀H₂₂ + C₂H₄ (b) Demand for smaller alkanes (petrol) and alkenes is greater than the supply from fractional distillation; long chains are less useful. (c) It can be used as a fuel or to make ammonia/margarine.

items.stem: A city plans to ban single-use plastic bags made of poly(ethene). (a) Give two properties of plastics that make them suitable for packaging. (b) Describe how PET is recycled. (c) Name the type of polymer PET is and its linkage.
items.answer: (a) Low density; strong; unreactive/does not corrode; waterproof; can be moulded. (b) Collected and sorted; cleaned; converted back into monomers (depolymerised) which are repolymerised into new PET (or melted and remoulded). (c) Condensation polymer — polyester; ester linkage.

items.stem: Jonas is given two solids, A and B. A contains CO₃²⁻ ions and B contains SO₃²⁻ ions, but the labels have fallen off. (a) Describe a test for sulfite ions and its result. (b) Write the ionic equation for the positive carbonate test. (c) Explain why the solution is acidified before testing with barium nitrate. (d) Name the gas produced in the test for nitrate ions and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) Add dilute hydrochloric acid, warm gently and test the gas with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII): sulfur dioxide produced, which turns acidified potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless. (b) CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O (c) To remove carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate (barium carbonate). (d) Ammonia: turns damp red litmus paper blue.

items.stem: A diagram shows a steel cell lined with carbon (the cathode) containing a molten electrolyte, with large carbon blocks dipping into it as anodes. (a) Write the half-equation at the cathode. (b) Calculate the mass of aluminium produced from 102 tonnes of aluminium oxide. (c) Explain why the molten aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell.
items.answer: (a) Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (b) 54.0 tonnes (c) It is denser than the electrolyte, so it sinks and is siphoned off.

items.stem: Write the word equation and the balanced symbol equation for the reaction of iron with dilute nitric acid. Include state symbols.
items.answer: iron + nitric acid → iron(II) nitrate + hydrogen; Fe + 2HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + H₂
items.markingKey: word equation [1]; formulae [1]; balancing [1]; state symbols [1]

items.stem: Diego investigates hydrated zinc sulfate, ZnSO₄·xH₂O. A 3.44 g sample is heated in a crucible; its mass is recorded after each heating: 2.61 g, 2.16 g, 1.93 g, 1.93 g. (a) Calculate the mass of water lost. (b) Suggest why a lid is placed loosely on the crucible. (c) Suggest how the calculated value of x would be affected if the sample was not heated to constant mass.
items.answer: (a) 1.51 g (b) To prevent loss of solid by spitting while allowing water vapour to escape. (c) x would be too small, because less water would appear to have been lost.

items.stem: A bottle in a school laboratory is labelled "but-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃". (a) Write the molecular formula. (b) State the general formula of this homologous series. (c) Calculate the relative molecular mass. (d) Name the next member of the same homologous series and give its formula.
items.answer: (a) C₄H₈ (b) CₙH₂ₙ (c) 56 (d) pent-1-ene, C₅H₁₀

items.stem: A village gets its water from a lake. Algae have covered much of the lake surface this summer and some fish have died. (a) Describe a chemical test for water. (b) State how you could show the treated water is not pure water. (c) Name two pollutants that might be found in the river and their sources.
items.answer: (a) Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns white to blue (or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride blue to pink). (b) Its boiling point would be slightly above 100 °C (or m.p. below 0 °C); evaporation leaves a residue. (c) Nitrates/phosphates from fertilisers; sewage from the town; metal compounds from industry; plastics from litter.

items.stem: Leila adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: bromine + potassium iodide; chlorine + potassium iodide; iodine + potassium bromide; bromine + potassium chloride. (a) State which of these mixtures react. (b) Use the results to put chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (c) Explain this order in terms of the electronic structure of the atoms. (d) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: (a) bromine + iodide; chlorine + iodide (b) chlorine > bromine > iodine (c) Down the group atoms have more shells; the nucleus attracts an extra electron less strongly, so the halogen gains electrons less readily. (d) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct mixture, no extras [2] (b) [1] (c) [2] (d) [1]

items.stem: A perfume company in Singapore purifies methanol from a mixture with propan-1-ol. (a) Explain why fractional distillation, rather than simple distillation, is used. (b) Describe what happens inside the fractionating column. (c) Suggest how the purity of the first fraction could be checked. (d) State one safety precaution. (e) Name one industrial process that uses fractional distillation.
items.answer: (a) The liquids are miscible with boiling points fairly close together; the column gives better separation. (b) Vapours repeatedly condense and re-evaporate on the glass beads; the more volatile liquid rises to the top. (c) Measure its boiling point: pure methanol boils sharply at 65 °C. (d) Heat with a water bath/electric heater if flammable; do not heat to dryness; use anti-bumping granules; goggles. (e) Separating crude oil into fractions (or liquid air).

items.stem: Name the apparatus used to measure the mass of a solid.
items.answer: A (top-pan) balance.

items.stem: Metal oxides are generally
items.answer: basic
items.markingKey: Metal oxides react with acids to form a salt and water.

items.stem: During a titration, Mateo overshot the end-point by adding acid too quickly. Predict the effect on the titre and explain.
items.answer: Titre larger: More acid than needed was added before the colour change was noticed.

items.stem: How many of these compounds are insoluble in water? lead(II) hydroxide, aluminium chloride, copper(II) chloride, zinc hydroxide, barium carbonate
items.markingKey: Insoluble: lead(II) hydroxide, zinc hydroxide, barium carbonate.

items.stem: Water samples from a coastal bay in Cape Town contain nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers. Explain why this is a problem.
items.answer: Cause eutrophication: algae grow, die and decompose, and bacteria use up dissolved oxygen so aquatic life dies.

items.stem: Propanoic acid has the structural formula CH₃CH₂COOH. Give the name and structural formula of one structural isomer of propanoic acid.
items.answer: methyl ethanoate: CH₃COOCH₃; ethyl methanoate: HCOOCH₂CH₃ (any one)
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct structural formula; 1 mark name [2]

items.answer: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻

items.answer: above 7

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why incomplete combustion of alkanes is dangerous in homes. (b) Explain why the reaction of methane with chlorine is called a photochemical reaction.
items.answer: (a) With too little oxygen, carbon monoxide forms; it is colourless, odourless and toxic. (b) It needs ultraviolet light to provide the energy to start the reaction.

items.stem: In the blast furnace, CO₂ + C → 2CO. What type of reaction is this?
items.answer: redox: carbon dioxide is reduced
items.markingKey: Carbon dioxide reacts with more coke to form carbon monoxide.

items.stem: A council in Bogotá is choosing between incineration and landfill for its plastic waste. Give one disadvantage of each.
items.answer: Incineration: produces carbon dioxide (greenhouse gas) and toxic gases such as hydrogen chloride from PVC. Landfill: plastics are non-biodegradable and take up space for hundreds of years.

items.stem: Sulfur dissolves in methylbenzene to form sulfur solution. What is the solute?
items.answer: sulfur
items.markingKey: solute sulfur; solvent methylbenzene; solution sulfur solution.

items.stem: State one reason why alloys are used instead of pure metals.
items.answer: Alloys are harder/stronger, or more resistant to corrosion, than the pure metal.

items.stem: Which gas bleaches damp litmus paper?
items.answer: chlorine
items.markingKey: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus (it may turn red first).

items.stem: While preparing sodium nitrate from sodium hydroxide and nitric acid, Lucas read the burette at the top of the meniscus. Explain why this is a problem and state how to correct it.
items.answer: Readings should be taken at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level, otherwise every reading is wrong/parallax error.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: effect on result/product; 1 mark: correct technique [2]

items.stem: Which balanced equation shows the reaction when photosynthesis takes place?
items.answer: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

items.stem: Deduce whether ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, and propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, belong to the same homologous series. Explain your answer.
items.answer: No: ethanoic acid is a carboxylic acid (–COOH (carboxyl)) but propan-1-ol is an alcohol (–OH (hydroxyl)).
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark functional group/general formula reasoning [2]

items.stem: A student tests metals P, Q, R with cold water and with dilute hydrochloric acid. items.answer: Q > R > P; Q could be sodium.
items.markingKey: Order Q > R > P [2]; identity consistent with observations [1]

items.answer: iron

items.stem: A company in Kathmandu must decide whether to make ethanol by fermentation or by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene. Compare the two methods in terms of raw material and energy use.
items.answer: Raw material: fermentation renewable (sugars from crops), hydration non-renewable (ethene from petroleum). Energy use: fermentation low, hydration high (high temperature and pressure).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each correct comparison for each factor (both methods) [4]

items.stem: A plant near Madrid electrolyses the alumina obtained from 200 tonnes of bauxite and produces 63.5 tonnes of aluminium. 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. Calculate the percentage by mass of aluminium oxide in the bauxite.
Answer both parts. (a) Compare the structures of nylon and proteins. (b) Explain why each monomer used to make nylon must have two functional groups.
items.answer: (a) Both have amide links; nylon is made from two different monomers (diamine + dicarboxylic acid) repeating, proteins from many different amino acids. (b) A functional group at each end lets the monomer link to two others, so the chain can keep growing.

items.stem: Sofia separates a mixture of ethanoic acid and hexane using fractional distillation. (a) Explain why fractional distillation, rather than simple distillation, is used. (b) Name one industrial process that uses fractional distillation.
items.answer: (a) The liquids are miscible with boiling points fairly close together; the column gives better separation. (b) Separating crude oil into fractions (or liquid air).

items.stem: Use the data to choose the most suitable material for electrical wiring and justify your choice. copper: density 8.96 g/cm³, conductivity 60 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $8.5/kg; stainless steel: density 8.0 g/cm³, conductivity 1.4 MS/m, corrosion — does not rust, cost $3.0/kg; zinc: density 7.14 g/cm³, conductivity 17 MS/m, corrosion — corrodes slowly, cost $2.8/kg; brass: density 8.5 g/cm³, conductivity 16 MS/m, corrosion — resists corrosion, cost $6.0/kg.
items.answer: copper: highest electrical conductivity.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why fertilisers must be soluble in water. (b) Explain why farmers should not spread lime (calcium hydroxide) on soil at the same time as ammonium fertilisers.
items.answer: (a) Plants absorb the ions in solution through their roots. (b) The alkali reacts with ammonium salts to release ammonia gas, so nitrogen is lost from the soil.

items.stem: Yusuf is given the structural formula CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ for an organic compound. (a) Write the molecular formula. (b) Name the homologous series and the functional group.
items.answer: (a) C₄H₈ (b) alkene; C=C double bond

items.stem: Element X is in Group III and element Y is in Group VII. X is aluminium and Y is fluorine. What is the formula of the compound they form?
items.answer: AlF₃

items.stem: Jonas compares 0.10 mol/dm³ propanoic acid with 0.10 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid by measuring their pH. Predict the result and explain it.
items.answer: The ethanoic-type acid has the higher pH (about 3 vs 1): propanoic acid is a weak acid, only partially dissociated, so lower [H⁺]; hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, fully dissociated.

items.stem: A greased steel bucket in Dubai is scratched, exposing the iron underneath. Predict whether the iron at the scratch will rust. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Yes: grease is only a barrier; where it is wiped off, water and oxygen reach the iron.

items.stem: Compare the refinery gas and lubricating oil fractions in terms of chain length, boiling point and where they are collected in the column.
items.answer: Refinery gas (C1–C4) has shorter chains, a lower boiling point and is collected higher up the column than lubricating oil (C30–C50).

items.stem: In a chromatogram, an unknown dye moves 8.0 cm and the solvent front moves 10 cm. The Rf values of known dyes in the same solvent are: F 0.45, C 0.50, D 0.65. Calculate the Rf of the unknown and deduce which dye it could be.
items.answer: Rf = 0.80; it does not match any of the known dyes.

(a) Calculate the mass of water lost. (b) Calculate the value of x. (c) Describe a test to show that the vapour given off is water.
items.answer: (a) 1.51 g (b) 7 (c) Condense it and add to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: white → blue (or cobalt(II) chloride paper blue → pink); pure water boils at 100 °C.

(a) Calculate the temperature rise for each metal. (b) Write the ionic equation for the reaction of magnesium with copper(II) ions. (c) Explain why silver gives no temperature rise. (d) State what is seen in the cup containing magnesium.
