The mixtures tested are: chlorine + potassium bromide; bromine + potassium iodide; iodine + potassium chloride; chlorine + potassium iodide. (a) Describe the colour change for the first mixture that reacts. (b) Explain this order in terms of the electronic structure of the atoms. (c) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: (a) the colourless solution turns orange as bromine is formed (b) Down the group atoms have more shells; the nucleus attracts an extra electron less strongly, so the halogen gains electrons less readily. (c) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic.

items.stem: Long-chain alkanes such as C₉H₂₀ are in low demand, so they are cracked: C₉H₂₀ → C₇H₁₆ + C₂H₄. (a) Write the balanced equation for cracking C₉H₂₀ into C₇H₁₆ and ethene. (b) Name the product formed when ethene reacts with steam, and give the conditions. (c) Suggest why hydrogen is also a useful product of some cracking reactions.
items.answer: (a) C₉H₂₀ → C₇H₁₆ + C₂H₄ (b) ethanol; phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C and 6000 kPa (60 atm) (c) It can be used as a fuel or to make ammonia/margarine.

items.stem: In a small smelter, 1000 kg of ore containing 80% SnO₂ by mass is heated with coke. (a) 1000 kg of ore contains 80% SnO₂. Calculate the maximum mass of tin produced. (b) Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted in the same way.
items.answer: (a) 630 kg (b) Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide; electrolysis is needed.
items.markingKey: (a) mass SnO₂ = 800 kg [1]; n = 5.30 kmol [1]; mass tin = 630 kg [1]; total [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: The monomer ethene is made from chemicals obtained from crude oil and is then polymerised. (a) Explain why ethene can form an addition polymer. (b) Draw (describe) the repeat unit of the polymer. (c) State one property that makes the polymer suitable for its use. (d) State the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation.
items.answer: (a) It has a C=C double bond (unsaturated). (b) –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ– (c) e.g. flexible/strong/waterproof/unreactive/electrical insulator. (d) Addition: only one product (the polymer); condensation: a small molecule such as water is also formed.

items.stem: Omar investigates the reaction of marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of carbon dioxide produced every 20 s. Results (time / s, volume / cm³): 0, 0; 20, 31; 40, 51; 60, 63; 80, 71; 100, 76. (a) Name the apparatus used to measure time. (b) Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 40 s. (c) State and explain how the rate changes during the experiment. (d) Suggest how the volume of acid should be measured, and why. (e) Suggest why the results become less reliable if the bung is not inserted quickly.
items.answer: (a) Stop-watch. (b) 1.28 cm³/s (c) Rate decreases: the concentration of acid (and amount of solid) falls, so collisions are less frequent. (d) Measuring cylinder is adequate (the acid is in excess) — or a pipette/burette for greater accuracy. (e) Some gas escapes before it can be collected, so readings are too low.

items.stem: Ana adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — iron: slow fizzing; a pale green solution forms; copper: no reaction; calcium: very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly. (a) Put the three metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction of calcium with hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: (a) calcium > iron > copper (b) Ca + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂

items.stem: Noah determines the concentration of sodium hydroxide by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.150 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, using thymolphthalein. Burette readings (initial → final, cm³): rough: 3.10 → 25.75; run 1: 3.10 → 24.75; run 2: 0.00 → 21.25; run 3: 1.05 → 22.70. (a) Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O (b) Explain why the rough titre is not included in the mean.
items.answer: (a) 0.130 mol/dm³ (b) It overshoots/ is only approximate.

items.stem: A chemical supplier in Karachi needs a sample of calcium sulfate, CaSO₄. (a) Name the most suitable method of preparation and explain your choice. (b) Name two aqueous reagents you could mix to make this salt.
items.answer: (a) precipitation (b) calcium nitrate and sodium sulfate
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: precipitation; 1 mark: reason (salt is insoluble) [2] (b) 1 mark each soluble reagent [2]

items.stem: Kenji visits a water-treatment works that supplies drinking water to a large city. (a) Describe the stages in treating the water to make it safe to drink, giving the purpose of each. (b) State how you could show the treated water is not pure water. (c) Suggest why chlorine is added at the end of the process.
items.answer: (a) Sedimentation and filtration — remove solids; carbon — removes tastes/odours; chlorination — kills microbes. (b) Its boiling point would be slightly above 100 °C (or m.p. below 0 °C); evaporation leaves a residue. (c) To kill microbes so the water stays safe in the pipes to homes.

items.stem: A chemist in Karachi separates two liquids, both with molecular formula C₃H₆O₂, from a mixture. (a) Name the compound CH₃CH₂COOH. (b) Give the structural formula of methyl ethanoate. (c) Calculate the relative molecular mass of C₃H₆O₂. (d) State the total number of structural isomers with formula C₃H₆O₂ that are listed in the coursebook and name any not already given.
items.answer: (a) propanoic acid (b) CH₃COOCH₃ (c) 74 (d) 3: propanoic acid, methyl ethanoate, ethyl methanoate

items.stem: Leila places a strip of magnesium into aqueous zinc sulfate. Mg + ZnSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Zn. (a) Write the ionic equation. (b) Write the half-equation for the change to the magnesium atoms. (c) Explain why the reaction would not occur if zinc were placed in a solution of magnesium ions. (d) Name the spectator ion.
items.answer: (a) Mg + Zn²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Zn (b) Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ (c) Zinc is less reactive; it has less tendency to form positive ions than magnesium. (d) sulfate ion

items.stem: Kenji watches a teacher add a small piece of rubidium to a trough of water containing a few drops of universal indicator. (a) Describe what would be seen when rubidium is added to water. (b) Predict how the melting point of rubidium compares with that of lithium. (c) A 0.390 g piece of sodium is used. Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at r.t.p. (d) Suggest one safety precaution needed for this demonstration.
items.answer: (a) reacts explosively; the indicator turns purple/blue. (b) lower: melting point decreases down the group (c) 203 cm³ (d) Use a very small piece / safety screen / goggles / tongs, not fingers.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per observation, max [2] (b) [1] (c) n = 0.390/23; ÷2; × 24 000 cm³ [3] (d) [1]

items.stem: A solution is tested: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate. The result is: white precipitate. Which ion is present?
items.answer: chloride (Cl⁻)
items.markingKey: chloride: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate → white precipitate.

items.stem: Which observation shows that excess magnesium carbonate has been added to dilute sulfuric acid?
options: Fizzing stops and solid remains in the flask
items.answer: Fizzing stops and solid remains in the flask
items.markingKey: No more CO₂ is produced and undissolved carbonate remains, so all the acid has reacted.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why farmers should not spread lime (calcium hydroxide) on soil at the same time as ammonium fertilisers. (b) Explain how overuse of fertilisers can harm rivers.
items.answer: (a) The alkali reacts with ammonium salts to release ammonia gas, so nitrogen is lost from the soil. (b) Excess soluble nitrates are washed into rivers, causing eutrophication and loss of oxygen for aquatic life.

items.stem: What is formed when aluminium burns in oxygen?
items.answer: aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃

items.stem: Describe the displayed formula of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH, stating the number and type of each bond that would be drawn.
items.answer: All atoms shown with every bond: 2 C–C, 5 C–H, one C=O, one C–O and one O–H bond; each C has four bonds; O has two bonds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark all bonds shown (each C four bonds); 1 mark correct bond counts [1]

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of aluminium that can be obtained from 2040 tonnes of pure aluminium oxide. (2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂)
items.answer: 1080 tonnes

items.stem: Which salt is formed when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
items.answer: sodium ethanoate

items.stem: Which property increases down the fractionating column?
items.answer: viscosity
items.markingKey: Down the column: longer chains, higher b.p., higher viscosity, lower volatility.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why copper does not react with zinc sulfate solution. (b) Explain why the sulfate ions are described as spectator ions in Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
items.answer: (a) Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc from its compound. (b) They are present in solution before and after the reaction and are not changed.

items.stem: Iodine dissolves in ethanol to form iodine solution. What is the solute?
items.answer: iodine
items.markingKey: solute iodine; solvent ethanol; solution iodine solution.

items.stem: Element Na has proton number 11. Deduce its electronic configuration, its group and period, and explain whether it is a metal or a non-metal.
items.answer: 2,8,1; Group I, Period 3; metal — it is on the left of the table and loses outer electrons to form positive ions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark configuration 2,8,1; 1 mark group and period; 1 mark metal/non-metal with reason [2]

items.stem: Three solutions X, Y and Z each contain one cation. Results — X: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; NH₃(aq) — white precipitate, insoluble in excess; Y: NaOH(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess; Z: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — no precipitate or very slight white precipitate. Identify the cation in each solution.
items.answer: X Al³⁺ (aluminium); Y Fe²⁺ (iron(II)); Z Ca²⁺ (calcium)

items.stem: State the general solubility rule for salts of sodium, potassium and ammonium.
items.answer: They are all soluble in water.

items.stem: Which method reduces sulfur dioxide emissions from power stations?
items.answer: flue-gas desulfurisation using calcium oxide
items.markingKey: CaO (a base) reacts with acidic SO₂.

items.stem: Bronze (copper and tin) is used for statues, medals and ship propellers. Explain why bronze is chosen instead of pure copper.
items.answer: Bronze is harder and stronger than copper; resists corrosion; pure copper is softer/weaker. The atoms of different size in the alloy stop the layers sliding.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: property of alloy relevant to use; 1 mark: comparison with pure metal / structural reason [1]

items.stem: A member of the alkenes contains 5 carbon atoms. What is its formula?
items.answer: C₅H₁₀

items.stem: Felix writes that in the extraction of aluminium "solid aluminium oxide conducts electricity". Explain why this is incorrect.
items.answer: In the solid the ions cannot move; it must be molten or dissolved in cryolite.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifying the error; 1 mark correct chemistry [1]

items.stem: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
items.answer: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O

items.stem: Which small molecule is eliminated when PET is formed?
items.answer: water

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how the oxide layer on aluminium can be made thicker, and why this is useful. (b) Explain why gold is found uncombined in the Earth’s crust.
items.answer: (a) By anodising (electrolysis with aluminium as the anode); the thicker oxide layer gives even better protection against corrosion and can be dyed. (b) Gold has very little tendency to form positive ions, so it does not react with oxygen, water or acids.

items.stem: A spot moved 4.8 cm from the baseline and the solvent front moved 8.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value.
Explain why the noble gases are placed in Group VIII (or 0).
items.answer: They all have full outer shells (eight electrons, or two for helium) and similar unreactive properties.

items.stem: In a titration, 10.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ potassium hydroxide required 15.20 cm³ of nitric acid for neutralisation. HNO₃ + KOH → KNO₃ + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.0329 mol/dm³

items.stem: When 6.15 g of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, is heated until all the water is removed, 3.00 g of anhydrous MgSO₄ remains. Calculate x.
Water samples from groundwater near an old factory in Muscat contain nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers. Explain why this is a problem.
items.answer: Cause eutrophication: algae grow, die and decompose, and bacteria use up dissolved oxygen so aquatic life dies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies harm; 1 mark explains how [2]

items.stem: What is the name of the ester formed from propan-1-ol and methanoic acid?
items.answer: propyl methanoate

items.stem: Magnesium is obtained by electrolysis of molten magnesium chloride, while zinc is obtained by reduction of the oxide with carbon. Use the reactivity series to explain the difference.
items.answer: Magnesium is above carbon and zinc is below carbon in the reactivity series. Metals above carbon need electrolysis; metals below carbon can be reduced by carbon; very unreactive metals are found native.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each metal positioned relative to carbon; 1 mark rule linking position to method [3]

items.stem: C₁₄H₃₀ is cracked to give C₁₁H₂₄ and one other product. Deduce the formula of the other product, write the equation and describe a test to show the product is unsaturated.
items.answer: C₃H₆; C₁₄H₃₀ → C₁₁H₂₄ + C₃H₆; add aqueous bromine: turns from orange to colourless.
items.markingKey: 1 mark formula; 1 mark balanced equation; 1 mark test and result [3]

items.stem: A country produces 2.40 million tonnes of plastic waste each year: 18% is recycled, 40% is incinerated and the rest goes to landfill. Calculate the mass sent to landfill each year and the total over 10 years, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 1.01 million tonnes per year; 10.1 million tonnes in 10 years; increase recycling / use biodegradable plastics / reduce single-use plastics.

items.stem: During a separation, Aisha sealed the end of the condenser with a bung. Explain what is wrong and how to correct it.
items.answer: Pressure would build up and could cause an explosion; the system must be open to the air.

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of iron in Fe(OH)₃ and hence name the compound using a Roman numeral.
items.answer: +3; iron(III) compound
items.markingKey: Oxidation numbers in a compound sum to zero; O = −2, Cl = −1, K = +1, SO₄ = −2, NO₃ = −1, OH = −1 [1]; iron = +3 [1]

items.stem: To prepare silver bromide, Isla evaporated the mixture to dryness instead of filtering. Explain the mistake and how to correct it.
items.answer: The solid would be contaminated with the soluble sodium nitrate; filter, wash and dry instead.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: why it is wrong; 1 mark: correction [2]

items.stem: Elena watches a teacher add a small piece of lithium to a trough of water containing a few drops of universal indicator. (a) Describe what would be seen when lithium is added to water. (b) Suggest one safety precaution needed for this demonstration.
items.answer: (a) fizzes steadily and floats; it does not melt; the indicator turns purple/blue. (b) Use a very small piece / safety screen / goggles / tongs, not fingers.

items.stem: Diego carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid; (2) heating copper(II) carbonate; (3) hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide. (a) Describe the test for the gas from reaction (2). (b) Suggest which gas should only be tested in a fume cupboard and why. (c) Describe how a gas that is less dense than air and insoluble in water could be collected. (d) Write an equation for reaction (1).
items.answer: (a) limewater turns milky (b) None of these is highly toxic, but good ventilation is still advised. (c) Over water in an inverted measuring cylinder, or by upward delivery, or in a gas syringe. (d) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂

items.stem: Elena titrates 20.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide with 0.200 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid using thymolphthalein indicator. Burette readings / cm³ — rough: initial 1.05, final 26.00; titration 1: initial 3.10, final 27.55; titration 2: initial 1.05, final 25.40; titration 3: initial 0.50, final 24.85. (a) Calculate the mean titre using the concordant results. (b) Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide. KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O (c) Explain why the rough titration is not used in calculating the mean. (d) Suggest one source of error that would make the titre too large.
items.answer: (a) 24.38 cm³ (b) 0.244 mol/dm³ (c) It is only to find the approximate end-point; the acid is added quickly so it usually overshoots. (d) e.g. air bubble in the burette jet / overshooting the end-point / reading the meniscus from above.

items.stem: Leila is investigating air pollution near a motorway and a coal-fired power station. (a) State the composition of clean, dry air. (b) Write an equation for the formation of carbon monoxide from the incomplete combustion of methane. (c) Suggest two ways of reducing the concentration of these pollutants in a city. (d) Explain how particulates (fine solid particles) is linked to the source you would expect near a busy road.
items.answer: (a) 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, about 1% noble gases (mainly argon) and 0.04% carbon dioxide. (b) 2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO + 4H₂O (c) Catalytic converters; low-sulfur fuels / flue-gas desulfurisation; more public transport/electric vehicles; renewable energy. (d) Incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels; traffic burns large amounts of fuel.

items.stem: Engineers are reviewing the materials used for electrical wiring in a new factory. (a) State the property of copper that makes it suitable for electrical wiring. (b) Explain how this property relates to the structure of copper. (c) Data: zinc density 7.14 g/cm³, corrosion — corrodes slowly; aluminium density 2.7 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion; copper density 8.96 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion. Identify the least dense metal and suggest one use that benefits from its low density. (d) Other than physical properties, suggest one factor that affects the choice of metal.
items.answer: (a) good electrical conductivity and ductility (b) Metallic structure: delocalised electrons give conductivity; layers of ions give malleability/ductility; oxide layer or alloying gives corrosion resistance. (c) aluminium; e.g. aircraft bodies or vehicle parts, to reduce mass (it also resists corrosion). (d) Cost, availability, ease of recycling, appearance or toxicity.

items.stem: A chemist in Lisbon separates two liquids, both with molecular formula C₅H₁₂, from a mixture. (a) Define the term structural isomers. (b) Give the structural formula of 2-methylbutane. (c) State the total number of structural isomers with formula C₅H₁₂ that are listed in the coursebook and name any not already given. (d) Suggest why the isomers can be separated by fractional distillation.
items.answer: (a) Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. (b) CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ (c) 3: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane (d) Different structures give different boiling points.

items.stem: Arjun sets up four test-tubes to investigate rusting and leaves them for one week. tube 1: an iron nail in boiled water covered with a layer of oil; tube 2: an iron nail in dry air with anhydrous calcium chloride; tube 3: an iron nail wrapped in a strip of copper, in tap water; tube 4: an iron nail wrapped in a strip of magnesium, in tap water. (a) State the conditions needed for rusting. (b) Write the word equation for rusting. (c) Suggest why a painted car body rusts quickly once the paint is chipped. (d) Describe how boiling the water and adding oil changes the conditions.
items.answer: (a) Water and oxygen both present. (b) iron + water + oxygen → hydrated iron(III) oxide (c) The barrier is broken; water and oxygen reach the iron; paint gives no sacrificial protection. (d) Boiling removes dissolved oxygen; the oil layer stops oxygen from the air redissolving.

items.stem: Methane, CH₄, is used as a fuel in homes in Auckland. (a) Name the toxic gas formed if the supply of air is limited, and explain why it is toxic. (b) Calculate the volume of oxygen needed to burn 100 cm³ of methane completely. (c) Describe the reaction of methane with chlorine, including the conditions and the type of reaction. (d) Write the equation for the reaction with chlorine to form a monochloro product.
items.answer: (a) Carbon monoxide: it reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen. (b) 200 cm³ (c) UV light; substitution — an H atom is replaced by Cl, forming a chloroalkane and HCl. (d) CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl

items.stem: The monomer phenylethene (styrene) is made from chemicals obtained from crude oil and is then polymerised. (a) Explain why phenylethene (styrene) can form an addition polymer. (b) Calculate the Mr of a chain containing 1000 monomer units. (c) Explain why the polymer is non-biodegradable.
items.answer: (a) It has a C=C double bond (unsaturated). (b) 104,000 (c) Microorganisms cannot break the strong C–C bonds of the chain; it is unreactive.

items.stem: Mei investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles; Q: cold water — reacts vigorously, fizzing and moving around on the surface; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; R: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing; S: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — reacts steadily with fizzing. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) P is iron. Write the equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid. (c) Predict what would happen if Q were added to a solution of copper(II) sulfate. Explain.
items.answer: (a) Q > R > S > P (b) Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂ (c) It reacts with the water first: fizzing (hydrogen) and an alkaline hydroxide forms, giving a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide; copper metal is not displaced.

items.stem: Aisha investigates the reaction of marble chips (calcium carbonate) with dilute hydrochloric acid by measuring the volume of carbon dioxide produced every 20 s. Results (time / s, volume / cm³): 0, 0; 20, 42; 40, 63; 60, 74; 80, 79; 100, 81. (a) Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 40 s. (b) State and explain how the rate changes during the experiment. (c) Suggest why the results become less reliable if the bung is not inserted quickly.
items.answer: (a) 1.58 cm³/s (b) Rate decreases: the concentration of acid (and amount of solid) falls, so collisions are less frequent. (c) Some gas escapes before it can be collected, so readings are too low.

items.stem: Lina adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: bromine + potassium iodide; iodine + potassium chloride; chlorine + potassium bromide; bromine + potassium chloride. (a) State which of these mixtures react. (b) Describe the colour change for the first mixture that reacts. (c) Use the results to put chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (d) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard. (e) Identify the reducing agent in the first mixture that reacts.
items.answer: (a) bromine + iodide; chlorine + bromide (b) the colourless solution turns brown as iodine is formed (c) chlorine > bromine > iodine (d) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic. (e) iodide ions (I⁻)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct mixture, no extras [2] (b) [1] (c) [1] (d) [1] (e) [1]

items.stem: A laboratory in Lisbon needs to confirm the anions present in two fertiliser samples. (a) Describe a test for iodide ions and its result. (b) Write the ionic equation for the positive chloride test. (c) Explain why the solution is acidified before testing with barium nitrate. (d) Name the gas produced in the test for nitrate ions and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate: yellow precipitate. (b) Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) (c) To remove carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate (barium carbonate). (d) Ammonia: turns damp red litmus paper blue.

items.stem: Calculate the minimum mass of magnesium, Mg, needed to react completely with 25.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ nitric acid. Suggest why a larger mass is used in practice. (Mg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂)
items.answer: 0.150 g; excess is used so that all the acid reacts and the salt is not contaminated with acid.

items.stem: Chloe prepares a sample of ammonium phosphate in the laboratory by titrating aqueous ammonia with phosphoric acid. (a) Explain why this fertiliser should not be mixed with calcium hydroxide. (b) State which other element(s) a farmer might need to add, and suggest a compound to supply it.
items.answer: (a) Calcium hydroxide is an alkali; it reacts with ammonium ions to release ammonia gas, losing nitrogen. (b) Potassium (e.g. potassium nitrate/sulfate).

items.stem: Noah adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — iron: slow fizzing; a pale green solution forms; magnesium: rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly and the tube gets warm; aluminium: slow at first (oxide layer), then steady fizzing. (a) Put the three metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) State two variables that must be kept the same to make this a fair test.
items.answer: (a) magnesium > aluminium > iron (b) Any two: size/mass/surface area of metal; volume, concentration and temperature of acid.

items.stem: A bottle in a quality-control laboratory is labelled "propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH". (a) Write the molecular formula. (b) Write the empirical formula. (c) Calculate the relative molecular mass. (d) Calculate the percentage by mass of carbon.
items.answer: (a) C₃H₆O₂ (b) C₃H₆O₂ (c) 74 (d) 48.6%

items.stem: Leila visits an aluminium plant where 102 tonnes of aluminium oxide are electrolysed each day. (a) Explain why cryolite is used. (b) Write the half-equation at the cathode. (c) Explain why the anodes must be replaced regularly, with an equation.
items.answer: (a) Aluminium oxide dissolves in molten cryolite at a much lower temperature than its melting point, saving energy; it also improves conductivity. (b) Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (c) Oxygen reacts with the hot carbon: C + O₂ → CO₂, so the anodes burn away.

items.stem: A food-flavouring company makes the ester ethyl ethanoate from ethanoic acid. (a) Explain why ethanoic acid is described as a weak acid. (b) Describe what is seen when calcium carbonate is added and write the equation. (c) Suggest a use of esters.
items.answer: (a) It is only partially dissociated into H⁺ ions in aqueous solution. (b) Fizzing; the solid dissolves; 2CH₃COOH + CaCO₃ → (CH₃COO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂ (c) Flavourings, perfumes or solvents.

items.stem: Diego draws a labelled diagram of a fractionating column showing where three fractions, fuel oil, diesel oil / gas oil, bitumen, are collected. (a) State which of fuel oil, diesel oil / gas oil, bitumen is collected nearest the top and explain why. (b) Give a use of diesel oil / gas oil. (c) State how volatility changes down the column. (d) Name the main constituent of natural gas and write the equation for its complete combustion. (e) Give one reason why burning fossil fuels causes environmental concern.
items.answer: (a) diesel oil / gas oil: shortest chains, lowest boiling point. (b) fuel in diesel engines (c) It decreases. (d) Methane; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (e) CO₂ is a greenhouse gas (climate change); SO₂ causes acid rain; CO/particulates from incomplete combustion.

items.stem: A technician needs a compound that is insoluble in water. Which one should be chosen?
items.answer: zinc carbonate
items.markingKey: Zinc carbonate (ZnCO₃) is insoluble: carbonates are insoluble except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates.

items.stem: Which piece of apparatus is rinsed with the alkali before it is used to measure 25.0 cm³ of alkali?
items.answer: the pipette
items.markingKey: Rinsing with the solution prevents dilution by water left inside.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why copper does not react with zinc sulfate solution. (b) Explain why the thermite reaction is used to weld railway lines.
items.answer: (a) Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc from its compound. (b) It is very exothermic; the iron produced is molten and fills the gap between the rails.

items.stem: Which balanced equation shows the reaction when sulfur dioxide is removed by calcium oxide?
items.answer: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why each monomer used to make nylon must have two functional groups. (b) Explain the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation.
items.answer: (a) A functional group at each end lets the monomer link to two others, so the chain can keep growing. (b) Addition: alkene monomers join, polymer is the only product. Condensation: monomers with two functional groups join, eliminating water (or HCl).

items.stem: 300 t of bauxite yields enough purified aluminium oxide to make 98.5 t of aluminium by electrolysis. 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. Calculate the percentage by mass of aluminium oxide in the bauxite.
Give one use of brass.
items.answer: Musical instruments, door handles, electrical plug pins or ornaments.

items.stem: A pure substance on a chromatogram gives
options: a spot on the baseline only
items.answer: one spot
items.markingKey: A mixture gives several spots; a pure substance gives a single spot.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain what is meant by "variable oxidation number", using iron as an example. (b) Explain why transition elements are useful in industry as catalysts.
items.answer: (a) An element can form ions with different charges in different compounds, e.g. Fe²⁺ in iron(II) sulfate and Fe³⁺ in iron(III) chloride. (b) They (or their compounds) speed up reactions without being used up, so less energy/lower temperatures are needed and costs fall.

items.stem: What is the relative molecular mass of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH?
Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why cracking always produces at least one unsaturated product. (b) Explain why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.
items.answer: (a) A long alkane does not have enough hydrogen atoms for all the smaller molecules to be saturated, so at least one alkene (or H₂) forms. (b) The C=C double bond can open up, allowing atoms to add across it.

items.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of water in hydrated cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl₂·6H₂O.
What is the test for carbon dioxide?
options: It pops with a lighted splint
It turns damp red litmus blue
items.answer: It turns limewater milky

items.stem: Which observation is expected when calcium is added to cold water?
options: reacts slowly with a few bubbles
fizzes steadily; the water turns cloudy as calcium hydroxide forms
items.answer: fizzes steadily; the water turns cloudy as calcium hydroxide forms
items.markingKey: calcium with cold water: fizzes steadily; the water turns cloudy as calcium hydroxide forms.

items.stem: Water samples from a river near farmland in Colombo contain nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers. Explain why this is a problem.
items.answer: Cause eutrophication: algae grow, die and decompose, and bacteria use up dissolved oxygen so aquatic life dies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies harm; 1 mark explains how [1]

items.stem: Put these fractions in order of decreasing boiling point: lubricating oil, naphtha, gasoline / petrol, refinery gas. Explain your order.
items.answer: lubricating oil > naphtha > gasoline / petrol > refinery gas; boiling point increases with chain length (fractions from lower in the column have longer molecules and stronger intermolecular forces).
items.markingKey: 1 mark order; 1 mark linked to chain length / intermolecular forces [1]

items.stem: Gold is obtained by collecting the native (uncombined) metal, while calcium is obtained by electrolysis of the molten chloride. Use the reactivity series to explain the difference.
items.answer: Gold is very low in the series (unreactive) and calcium is above carbon in the reactivity series. Metals above carbon need electrolysis; metals below carbon can be reduced by carbon; very unreactive metals are found native.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each metal positioned relative to carbon; 1 mark rule linking position to method [2]

items.stem: A 25 g key is made of stainless steel containing 15% chromium by mass. Calculate the mass of chromium and of the rest of the alloy.
items.answer: 3.75 g chromium; 21.3 g other

items.stem: How do you know when the point of crystallisation has been reached?
options: Crystals form on a cold glass rod dipped into the solution
items.answer: Crystals form on a cold glass rod dipped into the solution
items.markingKey: A drop on a glass rod crystallises as it cools.

items.stem: Element Ne has proton number 10. Deduce its electronic configuration, its group and period, and explain whether it is a metal or a non-metal.
items.answer: 2,8; Group VIII, Period 2; non-metal — it is on the right of the table and tends to gain/share electrons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark configuration 2,8; 1 mark group and period; 1 mark metal/non-metal with reason [2]

items.stem: Pentane has the structural formula CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. Give the name and structural formula of one structural isomer of pentane.
items.answer: 2-methylbutane: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃; 2,2-dimethylpropane: C(CH₃)₄ (any one)
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct structural formula; 1 mark name [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why wine left open to the air turns sour. (b) Explain why ethanoic acid reacts more slowly with magnesium than hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.
items.answer: (a) Bacteria oxidise the ethanol to ethanoic acid (vinegar) using oxygen from the air. (b) Ethanoic acid is a weak acid — only partially dissociated — so the concentration of H⁺ ions is lower.

items.stem: A teacher in Seoul demonstrates the preparation of iron(II) sulfate from iron(II) carbonate and 100 cm³ of sulfuric acid of concentration 1.50 mol/dm³. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction. (b) Describe how you would know that the solid is in excess.
items.answer: (a) FeCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂ (b) Solid remains undissolved and effervescence stops.

items.stem: A solution of an unknown salt is divided into three portions for testing. Describe how aqueous sodium hydroxide should be added, and why.
items.answer: A few drops at a time, then in excess, observing after each addition — to see whether any precipitate dissolves in excess.

items.stem: Air near a city centre during rush hour is found to contain raised levels of sulfur dioxide. Describe the likely source of this pollutant and explain one effect it has.
items.answer: Source: combustion of fossil fuels that contain sulfur compounds. Effect: acid rain, which damages buildings and kills trees and aquatic life.
items.markingKey: 1 mark source; 1 mark effect; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: A country produces 8.00 million tonnes of plastic waste each year: 25% is recycled, 20% is incinerated and the rest goes to landfill. Calculate the mass sent to landfill each year and the total over 5 years, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 4.40 million tonnes per year; 22.0 million tonnes in 5 years; increase recycling / use biodegradable plastics / reduce single-use plastics.

items.stem: A student sets up an iron nail painted all over, in tap water. Predict whether the nail rusts after a week, and explain your prediction.
items.answer: Does not rust: the paint is a barrier that keeps out water and oxygen.

items.stem: A lighting company in Mexico City uses argon in its products. (a) Explain why argon is unreactive. (b) Predict whether argon has a higher or lower boiling point than helium.
items.answer: (a) Its outer shell is full, so it does not need to lose, gain or share electrons. (b) higher
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) boiling point increases down the group [1]

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for the neutralisation of potassium hydroxide by nitric acid.
items.answer: KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O

items.stem: Suggest a method to obtain pure water from sea water and explain why it works.
items.answer: Simple distillation: water boils and is condensed, leaving the dissolved salts.

items.stem: Astatine is below iodine in Group VII. Use the trends in the group to predict its reactivity compared with iodine, giving a reason.
items.answer: Less reactive than iodine: reactivity decreases down Group VII.

items.stem: Deduce whether methane, CH₄, and ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, belong to the same homologous series. Explain your answer.
items.answer: No: methane is an alkane (C–C single bonds only) but ethanoic acid is a carboxylic acid (–COOH (carboxyl)).
items.markingKey: 1 mark conclusion; 1 mark functional group/general formula reasoning [2]

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol that can be made by fermenting 360 g of glucose. C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

A paint pigment manufacturer in Colombo makes lead(II) iodide by precipitation, starting from 25.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ lead(II) nitrate in a trial batch. (a) State the colour of the precipitate. (b) Write the ionic equation, with state symbols. (c) Name the soluble by-product that remains in solution. (d) Explain why lead(II) nitrate is used rather than lead(II) carbonate as the source of lead(II) ions.
items.answer: (a) bright yellow (b) Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻ → PbI₂(s) (c) potassium nitrate (d) Lead(II) nitrate is soluble so it provides free lead(II) ions; the alternative is insoluble.

items.stem: Kwame is given two solids, A and B. A contains SO₃²⁻ ions and B contains Cl⁻ ions, but the labels have fallen off. (a) Describe a test for sulfite ions and its result. (b) Write the ionic equation for the positive chloride test. (c) Name the gas produced in the test for nitrate ions and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) Add dilute hydrochloric acid, warm gently and test the gas with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII): sulfur dioxide produced, which turns acidified potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless. (b) Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) (c) Ammonia: turns damp red litmus paper blue.

items.stem: Grace notices that aluminium window frames in Bangkok have lasted for decades without corroding, even though aluminium is high in the reactivity series. (a) Explain why aluminium seems unreactive. (b) Write the half-equation for the formation of aluminium ions. (c) State whether aluminium is oxidised or reduced when it forms ions, giving a reason. (d) Suggest why aluminium is placed above zinc in the reactivity series even though it often reacts more slowly. (e) Write the equation for the formation of the oxide layer.
items.answer: (a) It is covered by a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that stops oxygen and water reaching the metal. (b) Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ (c) Oxidised: it loses electrons. (d) Once the oxide layer is removed, aluminium loses electrons more readily than zinc; its position reflects its tendency to form positive ions. (e) 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃

items.stem: Freya prepares a sample of ammonium phosphate in the laboratory by titrating aqueous ammonia with phosphoric acid. (a) Write the balanced equation for the formation of the fertiliser. (b) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium phosphate. (c) State which other element(s) a farmer might need to add, and suggest a compound to supply it.
items.answer: (a) 3NH₃ + H₃PO₄ → (NH₄)₃PO₄ (b) 28.2% (c) Potassium (e.g. potassium nitrate/sulfate).

items.stem: A factory in Lisbon makes poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE from tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂. (a) Explain why tetrafluoroethene can form an addition polymer. (b) Draw (describe) the repeat unit of the polymer. (c) State one property that makes the polymer suitable for its use. (d) State the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation.
items.answer: (a) It has a C=C double bond (unsaturated). (b) –[CF₂–CF₂]ₙ– (c) e.g. flexible/strong/waterproof/unreactive/electrical insulator. (d) Addition: only one product (the polymer); condensation: a small molecule such as water is also formed.

items.stem: A steelworks in Hanoi feeds 200 tonnes of hematite ore containing 70% iron(III) oxide into its blast furnace each day. (a) Describe, with equations, how carbon monoxide is formed in the furnace. (b) Write the equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide. (c) Suggest one use for the slag.
items.answer: (a) Coke burns: C + O₂ → CO₂; CO₂ reacts with more coke: CO₂ + C → 2CO. (b) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (c) Road building or making cement.

items.stem: Mei adds equal-sized pieces of three metals to separate tubes of the same volume and concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid. Observations — aluminium: slow at first (oxide layer), then steady fizzing; magnesium: rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly and the tube gets warm; calcium: very rapid fizzing; the metal dissolves quickly. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction of calcium with hydrochloric acid. (b) Describe how the gas could be collected and its volume measured. (c) Suggest a metal that would show no reaction with the acid and explain why. (d) Predict what would be seen if calcium powder were used instead of a piece.
items.answer: (a) Ca + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂ (b) Connect the tube to a gas syringe (or collect over water in an inverted measuring cylinder) and read the volume. (c) Copper (or silver/gold): it is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. (d) Faster fizzing (larger surface area) but the same total volume of gas for the same mass.

items.stem: Amara investigates the reaction of zinc granules with dilute sulfuric acid by measuring the volume of hydrogen produced every 20 s. Results (time / s, volume / cm³): 0, 0; 20, 27; 40, 43; 60, 54; 80, 61; 100, 65. (a) Name the apparatus used to measure the volume of gas. (b) Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 40 s. (c) Suggest how the volume of acid should be measured, and why.
items.answer: (a) Gas syringe. (b) 1.08 cm³/s (c) Measuring cylinder is adequate (the acid is in excess) — or a pipette/burette for greater accuracy.

items.stem: An encyclopaedia lists the properties of sodium (proton number 11), a Group I element. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction with water. (b) A 0.780 g piece of sodium is used. Calculate the volume of hydrogen formed at r.t.p.
items.answer: (a) 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ (b) 407 cm³

items.stem: Four organic compounds are: A CH₃OH; B CH₂=CHCH₃; C CH₃CH₂CH₃; D CH₄. (a) Name each compound. (b) Which compound(s) would turn aqueous bromine from orange to colourless?
items.answer: (a) A methanol; B propene; C propane; D methane (b) B

items.stem: Ana investigates the reactions of ethane, a member of the alkane homologous series. (a) Name the toxic gas formed if the supply of air is limited, and explain why it is toxic. (b) Calculate the volume of oxygen needed to burn 50 cm³ of ethane completely. (c) Describe the reaction of ethane with chlorine, including the conditions and the type of reaction.
items.answer: (a) Carbon monoxide: it reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen. (b) 175 cm³ (c) UV light; substitution — an H atom is replaced by Cl, forming a chloroalkane and HCl.

items.stem: Hana reads that sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄, is used in industry and wants to make some in the laboratory. (a) State whether sodium sulfate is soluble or insoluble in water. (b) Name the most suitable method of preparation and explain your choice. (c) Name the acid and the alkali you would use. (d) Explain why the titration is repeated without the indicator before crystallising.
items.answer: (a) soluble (b) titration (c) sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide (d) The indicator would contaminate the salt; using the known volumes gives a pure neutral solution.
items.markingKey: (a) all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble [1] (b) 1 mark: titration; 1 mark: reason (salt is soluble and made from an alkali, so an indicator is needed to find the end-point) [2] (c) 1 mark each [2] (d) [2]

items.stem: Yusuf determines the concentration of sodium hydroxide by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.100 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid, using thymolphthalein. Burette readings (initial → final, cm³): rough: 3.10 → 30.10; run 1: 0.00 → 26.35; run 2: 1.05 → 27.35; run 3: 0.80 → 27.20. (a) State the colour change at the end-point. (b) Explain why universal indicator is not suitable. (c) Suggest why a white tile is used. (d) Explain why the rough titre is not included in the mean.
items.answer: (a) blue to colourless (b) It changes colour gradually; no sharp end-point. (c) To see the colour change clearly. (d) It overshoots/ is only approximate.

items.stem: Zara adds 1.0 g of each metal powder to 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate solution in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature. Results — zinc: start 21.0 °C, highest 37.0 °C; copper: start 21.0 °C, highest 21.0 °C; iron: start 21.0 °C, highest 30.0 °C; silver: start 21.0 °C, highest 21.0 °C. (a) State two variables that must be controlled. (b) Explain why silver gives no temperature rise.
items.answer: (a) Mass/particle size of metal; volume, concentration and starting temperature of copper(II) sulfate. (b) Silver is less reactive than copper, so no displacement occurs.

items.stem: A car manufacturer in Colombo fits catalytic converters containing platinum and rhodium to all its petrol cars. (a) State two effects of climate change. (b) Suggest two strategies to reduce methane emissions.
items.answer: (a) Rising sea levels; melting ice caps; more extreme weather; changes in rainfall/crop growth; flooding; droughts. (b) Reduce livestock farming; capture methane from landfill; reduce food waste.

items.stem: Tariq compares the structures of protein and poly(ethene). (a) Name the type of polymerisation used to form protein. (b) State the monomers used to make protein. (c) Name the small molecule eliminated. (d) Describe the repeat unit using block diagrams for the carbon chains.
items.answer: (a) Condensation polymerisation. (b) amino acids (c) water (d) –[NH–CHR–CO]– (different R groups)

items.stem: An aluminium smelter in Kathmandu electrolyses purified bauxite dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950 °C. (a) Explain why cryolite is used. (b) Write the half-equation at the cathode. (c) Give two reasons why recycling aluminium is better than extracting it.
items.answer: (a) Aluminium oxide dissolves in molten cryolite at a much lower temperature than its melting point, saving energy; it also improves conductivity. (b) Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (c) Saves energy; conserves bauxite; less mining damage; less CO₂ from anodes and power generation.

items.stem: A company in Lima is choosing a metal for cutlery. (a) State the property of stainless steel that makes it suitable for cutlery. (b) Data: zinc density 7.14 g/cm³, corrosion — corrodes slowly; copper density 8.96 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion; aluminium density 2.7 g/cm³, corrosion — resists corrosion. Identify the least dense metal and suggest one use that benefits from its low density. (c) Suggest one disadvantage of using pure iron for an outdoor structure and how steel overcomes it. (d) Other than physical properties, suggest one factor that affects the choice of metal.
items.answer: (a) hardness and resistance to rusting (b) aluminium; e.g. aircraft bodies or vehicle parts, to reduce mass (it also resists corrosion). (c) Iron rusts and is soft; stainless steel resists rusting and is harder (or mild steel is stronger and can be painted). (d) Cost, availability, ease of recycling, appearance or toxicity.

items.stem: Hana uses paper chromatography to test a black ink. Known dyes blue, yellow, red are spotted next to the ink. The solvent front moves 12 cm. The ink gives two spots, at 5.4 cm and 8.4 cm; the known dyes travel blue 5.4 cm, yellow 8.4 cm, red 3.0 cm. (a) Calculate the Rf values of the two spots in the ink. (b) Explain why the baseline is drawn in pencil. (c) Explain why the solvent level must be below the baseline. (d) Describe how a colourless amino acid could be seen on a chromatogram. (e) Suggest why the Rf values must be compared using the same solvent.
items.answer: (a) 0.45 and 0.70 (b) Pencil is insoluble in the solvent and will not run. (c) Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent in the beaker. (d) Dry the paper and spray with a locating agent; spots become visible. (e) Rf values depend on the solvent (and temperature/paper).

items.stem: Which mixture would produce a displacement reaction?
items.answer: magnesium and zinc sulfate solution
items.markingKey: magnesium is more reactive than zinc: Mg + ZnSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Zn.

items.stem: What is the name of the ester formed from ethanol and ethanoic acid?
items.answer: ethyl ethanoate

items.stem: Compare the gasoline / petrol and lubricating oil fractions in terms of chain length, boiling point and where they are collected in the column.
items.answer: Gasoline / petrol (C5–C10) has shorter chains, a lower boiling point and is collected higher up the column than lubricating oil (C30–C50).

items.stem: Which balanced equation shows the reaction when the catalytic converter removes carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide together?
items.answer: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂

items.stem: Magnesium is obtained by electrolysis of molten magnesium chloride, while iron is obtained by reduction of the oxide with carbon (carbon monoxide) in a blast furnace. Use the reactivity series to explain the difference.
items.answer: Magnesium is above carbon and iron is below carbon in the reactivity series. Metals above carbon need electrolysis; metals below carbon can be reduced by carbon; very unreactive metals are found native.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each metal positioned relative to carbon; 1 mark rule linking position to method [2]

items.stem: A solid salt S is dissolved in water. Test 1: aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess. Test 2: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate: white precipitate. Identify salt S and explain how each result leads to your answer.
items.answer: iron(III) chloride: test 1 shows Fe³⁺; test 2 shows Cl⁻.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cation; 1 mark anion; 1 mark name of salt [2]

items.stem: Why is copper metal not used with dilute sulfuric acid to make copper(II) sulfate?
options: Copper forms a precipitate with the acid
Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not react
items.answer: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not react
items.markingKey: Cu does not displace hydrogen from dilute acids; use CuO or CuCO₃ instead.

items.stem: Halogens exist as
items.answer: diatomic molecules
items.markingKey: Each halogen is X₂, two atoms joined by a single covalent bond.

items.stem: Sipho compares 0.50 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid with 0.50 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid by measuring their electrical conductivity. Predict the result and explain it.
items.answer: The carboxylic acid conducts less well: ethanoic acid is a weak acid, only partially dissociated, so fewer ions in solution; hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, fully dissociated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark weak = partially dissociated; 1 mark link to H⁺/ions [2]

items.stem: Calcium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. What is the formula of the salt formed?
items.answer: CaCl₂

items.stem: In a college laboratory, Ravi timed a reaction by counting seconds out loud. Explain why this is a poor technique and suggest an improvement.
items.answer: Use a stop-watch for precise timing.

items.stem: Write the half-equation for aluminium atoms forming aluminium ions, and state whether this is oxidation or reduction.
items.answer: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻; oxidation (loss of electrons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark half-equation; 1 mark oxidation with reason [2]

items.stem: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂?
Which monomer is used to make PVC?
items.answer: chloroethene

items.stem: Water samples from groundwater near an old factory in Jakarta contain harmful microbes. Explain why this is a problem.
items.answer: Cause diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies harm; 1 mark explains how [2]

items.stem: A galvanised farm water trough in Bogotá is scratched, exposing the iron underneath. Predict whether the iron at the scratch will rust. Explain your answer.
items.answer: No: zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc loses electrons and corrodes instead (sacrificial protection).

items.stem: During a titration, Sipho added extra distilled water to the conical flask. Predict the effect on the titre and explain.
items.answer: Titre unchanged: The number of moles of alkali is unchanged, so the same volume of acid is needed.

items.stem: When 3.00 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, is heated until all the water is removed, 1.92 g of anhydrous CuSO₄ remains. Calculate x.
How does the character of the elements change from left to right across Period 3?
options: It alternates between metal and non-metal
items.answer: From metallic to non-metallic
items.markingKey: Na, Mg, Al are metals; Si is a metalloid; P, S, Cl, Ar are non-metals.

items.stem: Two unlabelled gas jars contain pentane and ethene. Describe a chemical test that would show which jar contains ethene, giving the result for each gas and explaining the difference.
items.answer: Shake each with aqueous bromine. Ethene: orange → colourless (addition across C=C). Pentane: stays orange (saturated, no addition).
items.markingKey: 1 mark reagent; 1 mark each result; 1 mark explanation [4]

items.stem: A mixture of hexane (b.p. 69 °C) and cyclohexane (b.p. 81 °C) is separated by fractional distillation. State which liquid is collected first, the thermometer reading while it distils, and how you would know when the second liquid starts to distil.
items.answer: hexane first, at 69 °C; the temperature rises again and stays constant at 81 °C when cyclohexane distils.
items.markingKey: 1 mark first liquid; 1 mark temperature; 1 mark sign of second fraction [3]

items.stem: Describe the displayed formula of butanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH, stating the number and type of each bond that would be drawn.
items.answer: All atoms shown with every bond: 3 C–C, 7 C–H, one C=O, one C–O and one O–H bond; each C has four bonds; O has two bonds.
items.markingKey: 1 mark all bonds shown (each C four bonds); 1 mark correct bond counts [2]

items.stem: A polypeptide is made from 300 molecules of the amino acid serine (Mr = 105). Calculate the number of water molecules eliminated and the Mr of the polypeptide.
Coal containing 3.0% sulfur by mass is burned. Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide produced from 500 tonnes of the coal. (S + O₂ → SO₂)
items.answer: 30.0 tonnes
items.markingKey: mass S = 3.0/100 × 500 = 15.0 t [1]; 32 t S gives 64 t SO₂, so mass SO₂ = 30.0 t [1]

items.stem: Mateo predicts that barium sulfate, BaSO₄, is soluble in water. Use the solubility rules to explain whether Mateo is correct.
items.answer: Mateo is incorrect: barium sulfate is insoluble because sulfates are soluble except barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct conclusion (insoluble); 1 mark: rule quoted (sulfates are soluble except barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates) [2]

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation number of iron in FeSO₄ and hence name the compound using a Roman numeral.
items.answer: +2; iron(II) compound
items.markingKey: Oxidation numbers in a compound sum to zero; O = −2, Cl = −1, K = +1, SO₄ = −2, NO₃ = −1, OH = −1 [1]; iron = +2 [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the waste gases leaving the top of the blast furnace include nitrogen. (b) Explain why carbon monoxide is described as the reducing agent in the blast furnace.
items.answer: (a) Hot air is blown in; the nitrogen in it is unreactive and passes through unchanged. (b) It removes oxygen from iron(III) oxide and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide.

items.stem: A solution of an unknown salt is divided into three portions for testing. (a) Predict what would be seen with aqueous ammonia. (b) Explain why a flame test would not help identify this ion.
items.answer: (a) red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess (b) This ion has no characteristic flame colour in the syllabus; use precipitate tests instead.

items.stem: Aqueous lead(II) nitrate is mixed with aqueous potassium iodide. Write (a) the balanced symbol equation and (b) the ionic equation for the reaction.
items.answer: (a) Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂ + 2KNO₃ (b) Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻ → PbI₂

items.stem: Helium is used for filling balloons and airships. Explain which property makes it suitable.
items.answer: It has a very low density and is unreactive (non-flammable).
items.markingKey: 1 mark property; 1 mark link to use [2]

items.stem: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of propan-1-ol.
items.answer: 2C₃H₇OH + 9O₂ → 6CO₂ + 8H₂O

items.stem: Duralumin (aluminium, copper and magnesium) is used for aircraft bodies. Explain why duralumin is chosen instead of pure aluminium.
items.answer: Duralumin is low density but much stronger than pure aluminium; pure aluminium is softer/weaker. The atoms of different size in the alloy stop the layers sliding.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: property of alloy relevant to use; 1 mark: comparison with pure metal / structural reason [2]

items.stem: Sulfur dissolves in methylbenzene to form sulfur solution. What is the solution?
items.answer: sulfur solution
items.markingKey: solute sulfur; solvent methylbenzene; solution sulfur solution.

items.stem: Tomás investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; Q: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; R: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing; S: cold water — fizzes steadily; the water turns cloudy as calcium hydroxide forms; dilute acid — reacts very vigorously. (a) Which metal(s) are below hydrogen in the reactivity series? Explain. (b) R is magnesium. Write the equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid. (c) Suggest how P could be tested with steam and what result you would expect.
items.answer: (a) P: they do not react with dilute acid. (b) Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ (c) Heat the metal strongly in a tube while passing steam over it; no reaction expected.

items.stem: A student plots the boiling points of the first five alkanes against the number of carbon atoms. Data: methane −162 °C; ethane −89 °C; propane −42 °C; butane −1 °C; pentane 36 °C. (a) State the general formula of the alkanes. (b) Predict the boiling point of hexane. (c) Which of these compounds are gases at 25 °C? (d) Give two other characteristics of a homologous series. (e) Write the molecular formula of hexane.
items.answer: (a) CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (b) About 69 °C (c) methane, ethane, propane, butane (d) Same functional group; similar chemical properties; differ by CH₂; same general formula. (e) C₆H₁₄

items.stem: A city plans to ban single-use plastic bags made of poly(ethene). (a) Give two properties of plastics that make them suitable for packaging. (b) Explain why plastic waste persists in the environment. (c) Describe how PET is recycled. (d) Name the type of polymer PET is and its linkage.
items.answer: (a) Low density; strong; unreactive/does not corrode; waterproof; can be moulded. (b) Most plastics are non-biodegradable; microorganisms cannot break them down. (c) Collected and sorted; cleaned; converted back into monomers (depolymerised) which are repolymerised into new PET (or melted and remoulded). (d) Condensation polymer — polyester; ester linkage.

items.stem: A farmer buys 25 kg bags of ammonium nitrate fertiliser for a wheat field. (a) Write the balanced equation for the formation of the fertiliser. (b) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate. (c) State which other element(s) a farmer might need to add, and suggest a compound to supply it.
items.answer: (a) NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃ (b) 35.0% (c) Potassium (e.g. potassium nitrate/sulfate) and phosphorus (e.g. ammonium phosphate).

items.stem: A diagram shows a steel cell lined with carbon (the cathode) containing a molten electrolyte, with large carbon blocks dipping into it as anodes. (a) Explain why cryolite is used. (b) Write the half-equation at the cathode. (c) Give two reasons why recycling aluminium is better than extracting it. (d) Explain why the molten aluminium collects at the bottom of the cell.
items.answer: (a) Aluminium oxide dissolves in molten cryolite at a much lower temperature than its melting point, saving energy; it also improves conductivity. (b) Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (c) Saves energy; conserves bauxite; less mining damage; less CO₂ from anodes and power generation. (d) It is denser than the electrolyte, so it sinks and is siphoned off.

items.stem: Elena carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) magnesium and dilute sulfuric acid; (2) ammonium chloride warmed with sodium hydroxide; (3) sodium sulfite warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid. (a) Describe the test for the gas from reaction (1). (b) Describe the test for the gas from reaction (2). (c) Write an equation for reaction (1).
items.answer: (a) a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop (b) damp red litmus paper turns blue (c) Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂

items.stem: Hana titrates 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide with 0.150 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid using methyl orange indicator. Burette readings / cm³ — rough: initial 0.80, final 22.20; titration 1: initial 0.80, final 21.10; titration 2: initial 0.80, final 21.60; titration 3: initial 1.20, final 21.90. (a) Calculate each titre and identify the concordant results. (b) Calculate the mean titre using the concordant results. (c) State the colour change at the end-point. (d) Describe how you would then obtain pure dry crystals of sodium chloride. (e) Suggest one source of error that would make the titre too large.
items.answer: (a) 21.40; 20.30; 20.80; 20.70 cm³; concordant: 20.80, 20.70 (b) 20.75 cm³ (c) yellow to orange/red (d) Repeat the titration with the same volumes but no indicator; heat the solution to the point of crystallisation; cool; filter and dry crystals. (e) e.g. air bubble in the burette jet / overshooting the end-point / reading the meniscus from above.
items.markingKey: (a) titre = final − initial for each [1]; concordant = within 0.10 cm³, rough excluded [1]; total [2] (b) mean of 20.80, 20.70 [1] (c) [1] (d) 1 mark each point [3] (e) [1]

items.stem: A video from a laboratory in Mumbai shows rubidium and caesium being added to separate troughs of cold water. (a) Describe what would be seen when rubidium is added to water. (b) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction with water.
items.answer: (a) reacts explosively; the indicator turns purple/blue. (b) 2Rb + 2H₂O → 2RbOH + H₂

items.stem: Propane, C₃H₈, is used as a fuel in homes in Karachi. (a) Write the balanced equation for complete combustion. (b) Describe the reaction of propane with chlorine, including the conditions and the type of reaction.
items.answer: (a) C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O (b) UV light; substitution — an H atom is replaced by Cl, forming a chloroalkane and HCl.

items.stem: Engineers are reviewing the materials used for water pipes in a new factory. (a) State the property of copper that makes it suitable for water pipes. (b) Explain how this property relates to the structure of copper. (c) Suggest one disadvantage of using pure iron for an outdoor structure and how steel overcomes it.
items.answer: (a) it does not react with water and is easily bent into shape (b) Metallic structure: delocalised electrons give conductivity; layers of ions give malleability/ductility; oxide layer or alloying gives corrosion resistance. (c) Iron rusts and is soft; stainless steel resists rusting and is harder (or mild steel is stronger and can be painted).

items.stem: Amara uses paper chromatography to test a black ink. Known dyes yellow, red, orange are spotted next to the ink. The solvent front moves 8.0 cm. The ink gives two spots, at 5.6 cm and 2.8 cm; the known dyes travel yellow 5.6 cm, red 2.0 cm, orange 2.8 cm. (a) Calculate the Rf values of the two spots in the ink. (b) Identify the dyes present in the ink. (c) Explain why the baseline is drawn in pencil. (d) Explain why the solvent level must be below the baseline.
items.answer: (a) 0.70 and 0.35 (b) yellow and orange (c) Pencil is insoluble in the solvent and will not run. (d) Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.

items.stem: Diego places a strip of iron into aqueous lead(II) nitrate. Fe + Pb(NO₃)₂ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + Pb. (a) Describe what would be seen. (b) Explain, in terms of electrons, which substance is the reducing agent. (c) Explain why the reaction would not occur if lead were placed in a solution of iron ions. (d) Name the spectator ion.
items.answer: (a) A grey solid forms on the metal. (b) Iron: it gives (loses) electrons to the lead ions. (c) Lead is less reactive; it has less tendency to form positive ions than iron. (d) nitrate ion

items.stem: Four organic compounds are: A CH₂=CH₂; B CH₃CH₂COOH; C HCOOH; D CH₃OH. (a) Give the functional group of compound A. (b) Give the molecular formula of compound B. (c) Name the ester that could be made from methanol and methanoic acid, and give its structural formula.
items.answer: (a) C=C double bond (b) C₃H₆O₂ (c) methyl methanoate; HCOOCH₃

items.stem: A refinery in Auckland separates crude oil by fractional distillation. (a) State which of refinery gas, diesel oil / gas oil, kerosene / paraffin is collected nearest the top and explain why. (b) Name the main constituent of natural gas and write the equation for its complete combustion.
items.answer: (a) refinery gas: shortest chains, lowest boiling point. (b) Methane; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

items.stem: Lucas reads a report about rising carbon dioxide and methane levels in the atmosphere. (a) Name two pollutants removed by a catalytic converter. (b) State two effects of climate change.
items.answer: (a) Carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen (also unburned hydrocarbons). (b) Rising sea levels; melting ice caps; more extreme weather; changes in rainfall/crop growth; flooding; droughts.

items.stem: A mining company in Dubai extracts zinc from an ore containing ZnO. (a) Write the balanced equation for the reduction. (b) 200 kg of ore contains 75% ZnO. Calculate the maximum mass of zinc produced.
items.answer: (a) ZnO + C → Zn + CO (b) 120 kg
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) mass ZnO = 150 kg [1]; n = 1.85 kmol [1]; mass zinc = 120 kg [1]; total [3]

items.stem: A student must plan tests to identify the anions in two unlabelled salts. (a) Describe a test for iodide ions and its result. (b) Write the ionic equation for the positive sulfate test. (c) Explain why the solution is acidified before testing with barium nitrate.
items.answer: (a) Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate: yellow precipitate. (b) Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) (c) To remove carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate (barium carbonate).

items.stem: A teacher in Kuala Lumpur demonstrates the preparation of magnesium sulfate from magnesium oxide and 40.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid of concentration 0.500 mol/dm³. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction. (b) Describe how you would know that the solid is in excess. (c) Calculate the number of moles of sulfuric acid used. (d) The percentage yield was 60%. Calculate the mass of crystals obtained and suggest one reason why the yield is less than 100%.
items.answer: (a) MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O (b) Solid remains undissolved. (c) 0.0200 mol (d) 2.95 g; e.g. some salt remains dissolved in the solution after crystallisation / losses on transfer.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balanced [2] (b) [1] (c) n = 40.0/1000 × 0.500 [1] (d) mass = 60/100 × 4.92 [1]; reason [1]; total [2]

items.stem: Elena adds aqueous halogens to aqueous potassium halides in a spotting tile. The mixtures tested are: chlorine + potassium iodide; chlorine + potassium bromide; iodine + potassium chloride; bromine + potassium chloride. (a) State which of these mixtures react. (b) Write the ionic equation for the first mixture that reacts. (c) Explain this order in terms of the electronic structure of the atoms. (d) Suggest why the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: (a) chlorine + iodide; chlorine + bromide (b) Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ (c) Down the group atoms have more shells; the nucleus attracts an extra electron less strongly, so the halogen gains electrons less readily. (d) Chlorine and bromine vapours are toxic.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct mixture, no extras [2] (b) [2] (c) [2] (d) [1]
